source: Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling, The 4 Disciplines of Execution (2012); Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan, Execution (2002)
opening: Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan wrote that execution is the great unaddressed issue in business: most strategies fail not because they are poor, but because they are not carried out. The team behind the Four Disciplines of Execution studied why, across thousands of teams, and found the enemy has a name.
idea: They call it the whirlwind: the urgent daily work needed to keep the operation running. Emails, crises, reports, meetings, requests from the boss. The whirlwind is necessary, and it consumes almost all available energy. New strategic goals, which require people to change behaviour, are constantly swallowed by it. The four disciplines are designed to carve out a small, protected space for what matters most. Discipline one: focus on the wildly important, one or two goals at most, each stated as 'from X to Y by when'. The more goals you have, they argue, the fewer you achieve.
mechanics: Discipline two: act on lead measures. A lag measure tells you whether you achieved the goal, such as revenue or audit findings, but by the time you see it, it is too late to change. A lead measure is predictive and influenceable: a behaviour that drives the goal and that the team can control, such as the number of client reviews completed each week. Discipline three: keep a compelling scoreboard, simple enough that anyone can see in five seconds whether the team is winning. People play differently when they keep score. Discipline four: create a cadence of accountability, a short weekly meeting in which each member reports on last week's commitments, reviews the scoreboard, and makes one or two new commitments for the coming week.
practice: Bossidy and Charan add that execution is the leader's most important job, not something to delegate. The leader must know the business, insist on realism, set clear priorities, follow through, and reward the doers. For anyone leading a strategy unit across several entities, the combination is practical: one or two wildly important goals per entity, lead measures you can track weekly, a visible scoreboard, and a fifteen-minute weekly accountability meeting that never gets cancelled.
faith: So when you have finished your duties, then stand up for worship, and to your Lord direct your longing. Mujahid and others explained it, as Ibn Kathir reports: when you finish your worldly work, turn to worship; when you finish one task, begin the next with effort. The verse describes a rhythm of continuous, directed effort, never idle, always aimed at Allah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the most beloved deeds are those done consistently even if small: a lead measure, practised weekly.
nigerian: The Yoruba say «Ọ̀rọ̀ púpọ̀ kì í kún agbọ̀n»: many words do not fill a basket. Nigeria has never lacked plans. Execution, with focus, measurement and follow-through, is what fills the basket.
practices: Choose one wildly important goal for the next quarter in the form 'from X to Y by date'.
Define two lead measures your team can control weekly.
Hold a 15-minute weekly accountability meeting for the next six weeks without cancelling it.
reflect: How many 'top priorities' do I really have?
Am I tracking only lag measures that tell me too late?
closing: When you finish one task, stand up for the next, and direct your longing to your Lord. Focus, measure, score and follow through.

verses.ar: فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَٱنصَبْ
verses.en: So when you have finished [your duties], then stand up [for worship].

verses.ar: وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَٱرْغَب
verses.en: And to your Lord direct [your] longing.

title: The Balanced Scorecard & OKRs
tag: What gets measured gets managed, so measure what truly matters.
source: Robert Kaplan and David Norton, 'The Balanced Scorecard', Harvard Business Review (1992); The Strategy-Focused Organization (2000); John Doerr, Measure What Matters (2018)
opening: In 1992 Robert Kaplan of Harvard Business School and the consultant David Norton argued that managing a company by financial numbers alone is like flying a plane with only one instrument. Their answer, the balanced scorecard, became one of the most widely adopted management tools in the world.
idea: Financial measures are lag indicators: they report the results of past actions. Kaplan and Norton proposed balancing them with three other perspectives. The customer perspective: how do customers see us? The internal process perspective: what must we excel at? And the learning and growth perspective: can we continue to improve and create value? Together, these four perspectives give a balanced view of performance and connect long-term strategy to short-term action. Their later work introduced strategy maps, diagrams that show the cause-and-effect chain: skilled and motivated people improve key processes, which delight customers, which produces financial results.
mechanics: A well-built scorecard has a small number of objectives in each perspective, each with a measure, a target and an initiative. The discipline is translating vague strategy into specific measures that people at every level understand. John Doerr, who learned the method from Andy Grove at Intel and brought it to Google, popularised a simpler cousin: objectives and key results. An objective is what you want to achieve, inspiring and qualitative. Key results are three to five measurable outcomes that show whether you got there. Doerr emphasises that OKRs should be ambitious, transparent across the organisation, and reviewed often. Grading them honestly, rather than hitting every target easily, is a sign of a healthy culture.
practice: Both tools carry a warning, often attributed to the economist Charles Goodhart: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. People optimise the number and lose the purpose. The best accountability systems combine numbers with judgement, review the measures themselves regularly, and keep the cause-and-effect logic visible so people remember why each number matters.
faith: And every person We have fastened his record to his neck, and We will produce for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open. Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant. Every human life has a scorecard, recorded with perfect accuracy and balance across every dimension: worship, character, family, wealth and knowledge. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said, in a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi, that a servant's feet will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about his life and how he spent it, his knowledge and what he did with it, his wealth and how he earned and spent it, and his body and how he used it. Four perspectives, balanced.
nigerian: In public institutions across Nigeria, performance contracts and dashboards have often measured activity rather than outcomes: workshops held, not lives improved. A balanced scorecard asks the harder question at every level: is our work actually producing the results our stakeholders need?
practices: Draft one objective and three key results for your unit for next quarter.
Draw a simple strategy map: people, processes, stakeholders, results.
Use the hadith's four questions as a personal monthly scorecard: time, knowledge, wealth, body.
reflect: Which number in my work has become a target that distorts behaviour?
If my record were opened today, which perspective would be weakest?
closing: Measure what matters, balance the perspectives, and remember that the most important record of all is fastened to your own neck.

verses.ar: وَكُلَّ إِنسَٰنٍ أَلْزَمْنَٰهُ طَٰٓئِرَهُۥ فِى عُنُقِهِۦ وَنُخْرِجُ لَهُۥ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ كِتَٰبًا يَلْقَىٰهُ مَنشُورًا
verses.en: And [for] every person We have imposed his fate upon his neck, and We will produce for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will encounter spread open.

verses.ar: ٱقْرَأْ كِتَٰبَكَ كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا
verses.en: [It will be said], "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as accountant."

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
tag: Your mind has two systems, and the fast one is in charge more often than you think.
source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011); Tversky and Kahneman, 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases', Science (1974)
opening: Daniel Kahneman was a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in economics. With his partner Amos Tversky, he spent decades showing that human judgement fails in systematic, predictable ways. Their work changed economics, medicine, law and public policy.
idea: Kahneman describes two modes of thinking. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it reads faces, completes the phrase 'bread and', and jumps to conclusions effortlessly. System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful: it does long division, checks an argument, and follows rules. We like to think System 2 is in charge. In reality, System 2 is lazy. It often accepts the quick story System 1 offers without checking. Most of our errors come not from stupidity but from trusting a fast impression where slow thought was needed.
mechanics: System 1 relies on heuristics, mental shortcuts that are usually useful but sometimes badly wrong. Anchoring: an initial number, even an irrelevant one, pulls later estimates towards it, which is why first offers matter in negotiation. Availability: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid recent events feel more probable than they are. Loss aversion: losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains please, which makes people cling to failing projects. Overconfidence and the planning fallacy: we underestimate how long and how costly projects will be. And what Kahneman called WYSIATI, what you see is all there is: the mind builds a confident story from whatever information is in front of it, without asking what is missing.
practice: Kahneman was pessimistic about fixing biases in individuals. Even he, after a lifetime of study, admitted he still fell for them. His hope lay in organisations, which can build procedures that slow decisions down: checklists, independent assessments, and what he called the outside view, asking how similar projects have actually turned out instead of trusting the inside story of this one. A compliance review, an investment committee or an audit is, at its best, a deliberate System 2 for the whole organisation.
faith: O you who believe, if a wrongdoer comes to you with news, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and then become regretful over what you have done. Ibn Kathir records that the verse was revealed about a report that a tribe had refused to pay zakah, which turned out to be false. The Qur'an orders a System 2 pause precisely when emotion and a convincing story push us towards fast action. The scholars of hadith built an entire science, 'ilm al-rijal, on this principle: no report is accepted on its surface; its chain and its narrators must be checked.
nigerian: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's talk, The Danger of a Single Story, is WYSIATI in human terms: when we know one story about a people or a person, we mistake it for the whole truth. And the Hausa say «Rashin sani ya fi dare duhu»: not knowing is darker than the night.
practices: Before any important decision, write down what information you do not have.
When estimating time or cost, ask how long similar projects actually took, not how long this one should take.
When a report makes you angry, apply the verse: verify before you act.
reflect: Which recent judgement of mine was really a fast story I never checked?
Where in my work does an early number anchor everything that follows?
closing: Your fast mind is a gift, but not a judge. Slow down where it matters, verify what you hear, and ask what you cannot see.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن جَآءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌۢ بِنَبَإٍ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓا۟ أَن تُصِيبُوا۟ قَوْمًۢا بِجَهَٰلَةٍ فَتُصْبِحُوا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ نَٰدِمِينَ
verses.en: O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.

title: Noise
tag: Two experts, same facts, different verdicts. That variability is a hidden cost.
source: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony and Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (2021)
opening: Bias is when judgements are consistently wrong in one direction. In their final major book, Kahneman, the strategy professor Olivier Sibony and the Harvard law professor Cass Sunstein argued that there is a second, largely ignored error: noise.
idea: Noise is unwanted variability in judgements that should be identical. Two underwriters pricing the same insurance risk, two judges sentencing similar offenders, two doctors reading the same scan, two analysts rating the same credit: in a fair and competent system, their answers should be close. In study after study, the authors found they were far apart. In one insurance company, executives guessed that two underwriters would differ by about ten percent on the same case. The actual median difference was around fifty-five percent. Wherever there is judgement, there is noise, and usually more than anyone expects.
mechanics: The authors break noise into parts. Level noise: some judges are simply harsher than others on average. Pattern noise: each person has their own idiosyncratic reactions to particular kinds of cases. And occasion noise: the same person judges differently depending on mood, fatigue, weather, or what came just before. One study they discuss found that judges' rulings varied with factors as irrelevant as the time of day. The cure they propose is decision hygiene: procedures that reduce noise without needing to know its direction. Use structured criteria. Break a judgement into independent sub-assessments before combining them. Have several people judge independently before discussing, so that the loudest voice does not anchor the rest. Use relative scales, comparing cases with each other, instead of absolute ones. And where possible, use simple rules or models, which are noise-free by design.
practice: This is directly relevant to any compliance, credit or investment process. If two officers would rate the same client's risk differently, the institution has a fairness and a regulatory problem, even if neither is biased. A noise audit is simple: give several people the same set of real cases, collect their independent judgements, and measure the spread. The result is usually humbling, and it shows exactly where guidelines and checklists are needed.
faith: O you who believe, be persistently firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both, so follow not desire, lest you not be just. Justice in Islam is not only about intention. It is about consistency: the same standard for the rich and the poor, the relative and the stranger. Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that Allah supports the just state even if it is unbelieving, and does not support the unjust state even if it is Muslim. Noise is a quiet form of injustice, because similar people receive different treatment by chance.
nigerian: For institutions in Nigeria, where trust in official decisions is often low, consistency is credibility. A regulator, a bank or a fund manager that treats similar cases alike, and can show its criteria, earns a legitimacy that no press release can buy.
practices: Write a short checklist of criteria for one recurring judgement in your work, such as client risk rating.
On your next committee decision, collect independent written views before discussion begins.
Run a small noise audit: give three colleagues the same two cases and compare their ratings.
reflect: Would two people in my team reach the same decision on the same file?
Do I judge differently when I am tired, rushed or irritated?
closing: Be firm in justice, and make it consistent. Structure your judgements, and let fairness be designed, not left to chance.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ شُهَدَآءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَوِ ٱلْوَٰلِدَيْنِ وَٱلْأَقْرَبِينَ إِن يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا أَوْ فَقِيرًا فَٱللَّهُ أَوْلَىٰ بِهِمَا فَلَا تَتَّبِعُوا۟ ٱلْهَوَىٰٓ أَن تَعْدِلُوا۟ وَإِن تَلْوُۥٓا۟ أَوْ تُعْرِضُوا۟ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرًا
verses.en: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allāh, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allāh is more worthy of both. So follow not [personal] inclination, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allāh is ever, of what you do, Aware.

title: Superforecasting
tag: Ordinary people who think like foxes outpredict the experts.
source: Philip Tetlock, Expert Political Judgment (2005); Tetlock and Dan Gardner, Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction (2015)
opening: For about twenty years, the psychologist Philip Tetlock collected tens of thousands of predictions from experts about politics and economics. His first finding was embarrassing: on average, the experts did little better than chance. His second finding was more hopeful.
idea: Some people predict far better than others, and the difference is not intelligence or credentials. It is how they think. Tetlock borrowed an image from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin: the hedgehog knows one big thing, and the fox knows many little things. Hedgehogs force every event into one grand theory and speak with great confidence. Foxes are sceptical of grand theories, gather information from many sources, think in probabilities, and change their minds when the evidence changes. Foxes forecast better. In a large tournament run by a United States intelligence research agency, Tetlock's team of volunteer 'superforecasters', ordinary people with this fox-like habit, beat professional analysts with access to classified information.
mechanics: Superforecasters share recognisable habits. They break big questions into smaller ones they can estimate. They start with the base rate, how often things like this usually happen, before adjusting for the details of the case. They express beliefs in precise probabilities, such as sixty-five percent, rather than vague words like 'possibly'. They update often, in small steps, as new information arrives, instead of either ignoring it or overreacting. And they keep score. Forecasts were measured with Brier scores, which reward accuracy and punish overconfidence. Tetlock found that keeping score, and reviewing what went wrong, is itself what makes people improve. Teams that debated respectfully did better than individuals.
practice: Most organisations never check their forecasts. Budgets, project timelines and risk assessments are made, and nobody later compares them with what actually happened. Tetlock's lesson for any strategy unit is to write predictions down with numbers and dates, and then review them honestly. Vague forecasts can never be wrong, which is exactly why they never improve.
faith: Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, sends down the rain, and knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Ibn Kathir explains, citing the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, that these are the five keys of the unseen which only Allah knows. This is the ultimate foundation for the humility of the fox. A believer plans, estimates and prepares, as Yusuf did for the seven years, but always says «in sha' Allah», because the future belongs to Allah alone. Overconfidence about tomorrow is a spiritual error as much as an analytical one.
nigerian: Hausa wisdom says «Abin da babba ya hango yana kwance, yaro ko ya hau rimi ba zai gani ba»: what an elder sees lying down, a child cannot see even from the top of a silk-cotton tree. Experience matters. But Tetlock adds a warning: experience only becomes foresight when you check your past predictions against what really happened.
practices: Write three predictions about your work for the next six months, each with a probability and a date.
Before estimating, ask: how often does this kind of thing usually happen?
When you change your mind on a matter, note why. That is a sign of good thinking, not weakness.
reflect: Am I more often a hedgehog or a fox?
Which of my past forecasts have I never checked?
closing: Plan with numbers, update with humility, keep score, and say «in sha' Allah». The unseen belongs to Allah; our duty is to think carefully about what He lets us see.

verses.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عِندَهُۥ عِلْمُ ٱلسَّاعَةِ وَيُنَزِّلُ ٱلْغَيْثَ وَيَعْلَمُ مَا فِى ٱلْأَرْحَامِ وَمَا تَدْرِى نَفْسٌ مَّاذَا تَكْسِبُ غَدًا وَمَا تَدْرِى نَفْسٌۢ بِأَىِّ أَرْضٍ تَمُوتُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌۢ
verses.en: Indeed, Allāh [alone] has knowledge of the Hour and sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. And no soul perceives what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul perceives in what land it will die. Indeed, Allāh is Knowing and Aware.

title: Mental Models
tag: Build a latticework of big ideas, and learn to think backwards.
source: Charlie Munger, 'A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom' (USC Business School, 1994); 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment' (Harvard, 1995); Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005)
opening: Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's partner at Berkshire Hathaway for decades, was famous less for any single investment than for the way he thought. In talks at business schools, including a famous lecture at Harvard on the psychology of human misjudgement, he described a method anyone can learn.
idea: Munger argued that you cannot really know anything if you just remember isolated facts. You need a latticework of mental models: the big ideas from the major disciplines, such as psychology, economics, mathematics, physics, biology and history, hung together so they support each other. Someone who knows only one discipline sees every problem through it; as the saying goes, to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail. With eighty or ninety important models, he said, you can handle most of the problems life brings. The goal is not cleverness. It is avoiding stupidity, consistently, over a long time.
mechanics: Several of his models have become classics. Inversion: borrowed from the mathematician Carl Jacobi, 'invert, always invert'. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid it. Circle of competence: know the boundaries of what you truly understand, and stay inside them, or admit when you are outside. Incentives: never underestimate their power; if you want to predict behaviour, look at how people are paid. Second-order thinking: ask 'and then what?' about every decision. Margin of safety: leave room for error, because you will be wrong sometimes. And the combination of several psychological tendencies at once, which he called the lollapalooza effect, explains why groups sometimes behave in wildly irrational ways.
practice: Inversion is powerful in compliance and risk work. Instead of asking 'how do we stay compliant?', ask 'what would be the surest way to end up in front of the regulator?' The answers, such as poor records, unchecked conflicts of interest, silence about small breaches, become a precise list of controls. Munger's habit of reading widely, across fields, is also a discipline: he said he knew no wise person who did not read all the time.
faith: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, about all of those one will be questioned. Ibn Kathir explains it as a prohibition on speaking or judging without knowledge, whether by suspicion or guesswork. This is the circle of competence as a religious duty. The classical scholars modelled the latticework too. Ibn Khaldun, in his Muqaddimah, combined history, economics, sociology and theology to explain how states rise and fall. Imam al-Shafi'i combined language, hadith and reason to found the science of usul al-fiqh.
nigerian: Nigeria's problems rarely respect disciplinary boundaries: an energy question is also a currency, security and politics question. A Nigerian leader with a latticework of models, faith, economics, history and the psychology of people, is equipped for problems a specialist cannot even see.
practices: For your current biggest decision, ask: what would guarantee failure? Then avoid those things.
Draw the boundary of your circle of competence, and name one decision this month that lies outside it.
Read one book outside your profession this quarter, and note one model it gives you.
reflect: What incentives are shaping the behaviour I am trying to change?
Where am I speaking with confidence outside my knowledge?
closing: Gather the big ideas, think backwards, stay inside what you know, and do not pursue what you have no knowledge of.

verses.ar: وَلَا تَقْفُ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلْمٌ إِنَّ ٱلسَّمْعَ وَٱلْبَصَرَ وَٱلْفُؤَادَ كُلُّ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْـُٔولًا
verses.en: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.

title: Thinking in Bets
tag: A good decision can have a bad outcome. Stop judging decisions by results alone.
source: Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets (2018); How to Decide (2020); Quit (2022)
opening: Annie Duke was a champion professional poker player who studied cognitive psychology at graduate level. Poker taught her something most executives never learn: you can play a hand perfectly and still lose, and play it badly and still win.
idea: Duke's central concept is 'resulting': judging the quality of a decision by the quality of its outcome. It is the most common error in organisational life. A manager who approved a sound investment that failed because of an unforeseeable event is blamed; a manager who took a reckless gamble that happened to work is promoted. Over time, resulting teaches people the wrong lessons. Duke argues that life is more like poker than chess. Chess has complete information and little luck. Life has hidden information and a great deal of luck. So every decision is a bet on an uncertain future, and should be judged by the quality of the thinking, the information and the options at the time it was made.
mechanics: Thinking in bets changes how you speak and decide. Instead of 'I'm sure', ask 'how sure, and what would I bet on it?' This simple question exposes overconfidence. Instead of reviewing only failures, review successes too, separating skill from luck in both. Duke recommends a 'decision group' of people committed to accuracy over comfort, who reward each other for honest self-assessment rather than for good outcomes. She also uses premortems: imagine the decision has failed a year from now, and list the reasons why. And she argues that quitting, at the right time, is a skill. Most people persist too long with failing projects because they cannot bear the sunk cost.
practice: For any committee or board, the lesson is to keep a record of why decisions were made: what was known, what was assumed, and what alternatives were considered. Then, when outcomes arrive, the decision can be evaluated fairly. This protects good decision-makers from being punished for bad luck, and stops the organisation from rewarding lucky recklessness.
faith: Perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. Allah knows, while you know not. This verse dissolves resulting at its root. The believer is accountable for his intention, his effort and his choice of means. The outcome belongs to Allah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught us istikharah for decisions, asking Allah to choose what is best, and taught that after taking the means, we rely on Him. If the result is not what we hoped, we say «qaddara Allah wa ma sha'a fa'al», Allah decreed and did what He willed, as in the hadith in Sahih Muslim, and we do not say 'if only'.
nigerian: In Nigeria's volatile environment, with sudden policy shifts and currency moves, good decisions often produce bad outcomes for reasons nobody could control. Leaders who judge their teams by the quality of decisions, not just results, build people who keep thinking clearly through the turbulence.
practices: For your next significant decision, write one paragraph: what I know, what I assume, and what I chose and why.
Run a premortem before launching a project: it failed, so why?
Pray istikharah for one important pending decision this week.
reflect: Have I blamed someone, including myself, for a good decision that met bad luck?
Which project am I continuing only because of what I have already spent on it?
closing: Judge the decision, not the dice. Think carefully, take the means, ask Allah to choose, and accept His decree with a calm heart.

verses.ar: كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْقِتَالُ وَهُوَ كُرْهٌ لَّكُمْ وَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تَكْرَهُوا۟ شَيْـًٔا وَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ وَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تُحِبُّوا۟ شَيْـًٔا وَهُوَ شَرٌّ لَّكُمْ وَٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَأَنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
verses.en: Battle has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.

title: Black Swans & Antifragility
tag: Some things break under shocks, some survive them, and some grow stronger.
source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan (2007); Antifragile (2012); Skin in the Game (2018)
opening: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, a former options trader turned philosopher of risk, spent his career attacking the false precision of financial models. The 2008 financial crisis, which most models said was nearly impossible, made his ideas famous.
idea: A Black Swan is an event that is rare, has extreme impact, and is explained afterwards as if it had been predictable. Wars, pandemics, crashes, a sudden currency collapse. Taleb argues that history is driven far more by these rare events than by the normal fluctuations our models measure. Since we cannot predict them, the right question is not 'what will happen?' but 'how exposed am I if something extreme happens?' This leads to his most important idea: antifragility. Fragile things break under stress, like a glass. Robust things resist stress, like a rock. But antifragile things gain from stress, disorder and volatility, like muscles that grow from exercise or an immune system strengthened by exposure.
mechanics: Taleb offers several practical principles. The barbell strategy: keep most of your resources extremely safe, and a small portion in high-upside experiments, avoiding the risky middle. Redundancy: keep reserves, savings and spare capacity, which look inefficient in normal times and save you in crises. Via negativa: improvement often comes more from removing harmful things, such as debt, bad habits or toxic relationships, than from adding new ones. Optionality: prefer positions with limited downside and open-ended upside. And skin in the game: never trust advice from people who do not bear the consequences of being wrong. Systems become fragile when those who take the risks are not the ones who pay for failures.
practice: For a fund manager or a compliance officer, Taleb's thinking challenges comfortable assumptions. A portfolio that performs well in normal years may hide a catastrophic exposure to one rare event. A company running at maximum efficiency with no cash buffer is fragile. Stress-testing, holding reserves, avoiding excessive leverage, and insisting that decision-makers share in the downside are the institutional forms of antifragility. Islamic finance's preference for risk-sharing over interest-based debt is, in Taleb's language, a principle of skin in the game.
faith: He entered his garden while wronging himself. He said: I do not think this will ever perish, and I do not think the Hour will ever come. The owner of the two gardens in Surah al-Kahf is the portrait of fragility: total confidence that the good years will last. One night, everything was destroyed. Yusuf, by contrast, built antifragility into Egypt: store in the seven good years for the seven hard ones. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told the man who asked whether to trust Allah or tie his camel: tie it, and trust in Allah, in a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi. Preparation and reliance on Allah belong together.
nigerian: The Yoruba say «Ilé ọba tó jó, ẹwà ló bù kún un»: when the king's palace burns, it is rebuilt more beautiful. That is antifragility in one line. Nigerian traders and families who survived repeated currency shocks often did so through Taleb's principles: diversified income, low debt, and networks of mutual support.
practices: List the three events that would hurt you or your organisation most, and one buffer for each.
Remove one fragility this month: a debt, a single point of failure, or a harmful habit.
Before taking advice, ask: does this person bear any cost if they are wrong?
reflect: Am I fragile, robust or antifragile in my finances, career and health?
Where am I acting like the owner of the garden, sure that the good times will last?
closing: You cannot predict the storm, but you can prepare for it. Tie your camel, store for the lean years, and trust in Allah.

verses.ar: وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُۥ وَهُوَ ظَالِمٌ لِّنَفْسِهِۦ قَالَ مَآ أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أَبَدًا
verses.en: And he entered his garden while he was unjust to himself. He said, "I do not think that this will perish - ever.

verses.ar: وَمَآ أَظُنُّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ قَآئِمَةً وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّى لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِّنْهَا مُنقَلَبًا
verses.en: And I do not think the Hour will occur. And even if I should be brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return."

title: Hausa Proverbs for Life
author: Karin magana · Hausa oral tradition
tag: Short sayings from northern Nigeria that carry centuries of practical wisdom.
ideas: «Sannu sannu bai hana zuwa»

Slowly, slowly does not stop you from arriving. Steady progress beats hurried bursts. In an age that wants results overnight, this proverb reminds us that patience and consistency carry people furthest.
«Haƙuri maganin duniya»
Patience is the medicine of the world. Many problems in family, business and community are solved not by force or cleverness but by the willingness to wait, endure and respond calmly.
«Komai nisan dare, gari zai waye»
However long the night, the dawn will come. Hard seasons end. The proverb has carried families through drought, loss and hardship, and it echoes the Qur'anic promise that with hardship comes ease.
«Hannu ɗaya ba ya ɗaukar jinka»
One hand cannot lift a thatched roof. Great work requires many hands. A leader who tries to do everything alone will eventually be crushed by the weight.
«Ɗan hakin da ka raina, shi ke tsone maka ido»
The little blade of grass you look down on is the one that pokes your eye. Small risks and small people deserve respect. Many disasters begin with something someone dismissed as minor.
«Rashin sani ya fi dare duhu»
Not knowing is darker than the night. Ignorance leaves a person stumbling even in daylight. The proverb has long encouraged learning, from Qur'anic schools to universities.
faith: Have you not considered how Allah presents an example, making a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches high in the sky? It produces its fruit all the time, by permission of its Lord. A good proverb is a good word with deep roots: short, memorable and fruitful across generations. Hausa wisdom grew alongside centuries of Islamic learning in the region, and many sayings carry the spirit of the Qur'an and Sunnah.
practices: Learn one proverb by heart and use it in conversation this week.
Teach a proverb to your children, with its meaning and a story.
Choose one proverb as your guide for a current challenge.
reflect: Which proverb describes the season I'm in now?
What small 'blade of grass' am I ignoring?
closing: Good words are good trees. Keep the wisdom of the elders alive, and let it bear fruit in your life.

verses.ar: أَلَمْ تَرَ كَيْفَ ضَرَبَ ٱللَّهُ مَثَلًا كَلِمَةً طَيِّبَةً كَشَجَرَةٍ طَيِّبَةٍ أَصْلُهَا ثَابِتٌ وَفَرْعُهَا فِى ٱلسَّمَآءِ
verses.en: Have you not considered how Allāh presents an example, [making] a good word like a good tree, whose root is firmly fixed and its branches [high] in the sky?

verses.ar: تُؤْتِىٓ أُكُلَهَا كُلَّ حِينٍۭ بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهَا وَيَضْرِبُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْأَمْثَالَ لِلنَّاسِ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَتَذَكَّرُونَ
verses.en: It produces its fruit all the time, by permission of its Lord. And Allāh presents examples for the people that perhaps they will be reminded.

deep: In Hausa culture, this proverb is often used to encourage patience in learning, business and building relationships. It reminds people that steady progress, even if slow, eventually leads to success, and it echoes the prophetic teaching that consistent small deeds are most beloved to Allah.

This proverb suggests that patience can resolve many problems that force or haste cannot. It is often quoted in family disputes, business setbacks and community conflicts, encouraging people to remain calm and wait for the right moment.
Used in times of hardship, this proverb offers hope that difficulties will pass. It reflects the Qur'anic assurance that with hardship comes ease, encouraging resilience and trust in Allah.
This proverb highlights the importance of cooperation. In leadership, it reminds people to build teams and share responsibilities, since no individual can carry heavy burdens alone.
It warns against underestimating small risks or people. In business and compliance, minor issues can become major problems if ignored, so vigilance and respect for details matter.
This proverb stresses the value of knowledge. It has been used to encourage learning in Qur'anic schools and modern education, showing that ignorance can lead to serious mistakes.

title: Yoruba Proverbs for Life
author: Òwe · Yoruba oral tradition
tag: The Yoruba say proverbs are the horses of speech: when words get lost, proverbs find them.
ideas: «Iṣẹ́ l'òògùn ìṣẹ́»
Work is the medicine for poverty. There is no shortcut around honest effort. The proverb has encouraged generations of traders, farmers and professionals to rise through diligence.
«Ìwà l'ẹ̀sìn»
Character is religion. A person's faith is seen in their conduct. Prayer without good character, the proverb suggests, is incomplete.
«Ọ̀rọ̀ púpọ̀ kì í kún agbọ̀n»
Many words do not fill a basket. Talk is not achievement. Meetings, speeches and plans mean nothing until something is actually done.
«Àjèjé ọwọ́ kan kò gbé ẹrù dórí»
A single hand cannot lift a load onto the head. Cooperation is necessary for anything heavy. Communities and teams rise when people help one another.
«Ilé ọba tó jó, ẹwà ló bù kún un»
When the king's palace burns, it is rebuilt more beautiful. Loss can lead to renewal. Setbacks are not the end; they can be the start of something better.
«Ọmọ tí a kò kọ́ ni yóò gbé ilé tí a kọ́ tà»
The child we fail to train will sell the house we built. Investing in children's character is more important than building wealth for them.
faith: And We had certainly given Luqman wisdom and said: be grateful to Allah. Wisdom, hikmah, is given by Allah to whom He wills, and it is not confined to one people. Luqman was honoured in the Qur'an for wise sayings to his son. Many Yoruba proverbs, on character, work and raising children, sit comfortably beside Luqman's advice.
practices: Use 'Ìwà l'ẹ̀sìn' as a test for one decision this week: does it reflect good character?
Turn one long plan into one concrete action today.
Share one proverb with a younger person, and explain it.
reflect: Is my character preaching my religion well?
What 'burned palace' in my life could be rebuilt more beautiful?
closing: Character is religion, work is medicine, and wisdom is a gift from Allah. Speak it, and live it.

verses.ar: وَلَقَدْ ءَاتَيْنَا لُقْمَٰنَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ أَنِ ٱشْكُرْ لِلَّهِ وَمَن يَشْكُرْ فَإِنَّمَا يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِۦ وَمَن كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ غَنِىٌّ حَمِيدٌ
verses.en: And We had certainly given Luqmān wisdom [and said], "Be grateful to Allāh." And whoever is grateful is grateful for [the benefit of] himself. And whoever denies [His favor] - then indeed, Allāh is Free of need and Praiseworthy.

deep: This proverb is often used to encourage diligence and self-reliance. It reminds people that consistent effort is the remedy for poverty and dependency.
It emphasises that a person's religion is reflected in their character. Good behaviour, honesty and kindness are seen as the true signs of faith.
This proverb criticises empty talk without action. It encourages people to follow through on their plans and promises, as results matter more than words.
It highlights the need for cooperation. Heavy tasks require collective effort, and communities thrive when people help each other.
The proverb suggests that misfortune can lead to renewal. Setbacks may create opportunities for rebuilding something better.
It warns parents and leaders that failing to train the next generation can undo their achievements. Investing in children's character and education is essential.

title: Igbo Proverbs for Life
author: Ilu · Igbo oral tradition
tag: Achebe wrote that among the Igbo, proverbs are the palm-oil with which words are eaten.
ideas: «Egbe bere, ugo bere»
Let the kite perch and let the eagle perch. Live and let live: there is room for everyone to thrive. Whichever denies the other room, may its wing break, the full saying adds.
«Onye ajụjụ anaghị efu ụzọ»
The one who asks questions does not lose his way. Humility to ask is the beginning of knowledge and good decisions.
«Ezi aha ka ego»
A good name is better than wealth. Reputation, built over years, opens doors that money cannot, and once lost, money cannot buy it back.
«Igwe bụ ike»
The multitude is strength. Unity and collective effort make communities powerful. Division makes even the strong weak.
«Onye wetara ọjị wetara ndụ»
He who brings kola brings life. Hospitality and generosity open relationships. In Igbo custom, sharing kola nut begins every important gathering.
«Nwata kwọchaa aka, o soro ndị okenye rie nri»
When a child washes his hands, he eats with elders. Earn your place through preparation and good conduct, and you will be welcomed among the respected.
faith: He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever has been given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will remember except those of understanding. Wisdom is a gift of Allah wherever it is found. The Prophet, peace be upon him, is reported to have said that a word of wisdom is the lost property of the believer; wherever he finds it, he has the most right to it, a narration recorded by al-Tirmidhi, though scholars grade its chain as weak; its meaning is widely accepted.
practices: Ask one more question than usual in your next important meeting.
Protect your good name in one decision where money tempts you.
Welcome a guest or colleague with generous hospitality this week.
reflect: Where am I denying someone else room to perch?
Is my name worth more than my wealth?
closing: Wisdom is the believer's lost property. Gather it from every people, and let it make you better.

verses.ar: يُؤْتِى ٱلْحِكْمَةَ مَن يَشَآءُ وَمَن يُؤْتَ ٱلْحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِىَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا وَمَا يَذَّكَّرُ إِلَّآ أُو۟لُوا۟ ٱلْأَلْبَٰبِ
verses.en: He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever has been given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will remember except those of understanding.

deep: This proverb promotes mutual respect and coexistence. It reminds people to allow others space to succeed, discouraging envy and exclusion.
It encourages curiosity and humility. Asking questions helps people learn, avoid mistakes and make better decisions.
This proverb stresses the value of reputation. A good name, built on honesty and integrity, opens doors that money cannot.
It highlights the strength found in unity. Communities and organisations achieve more when people work together.
Sharing kola nut symbolises hospitality and goodwill. This proverb reminds people that generosity builds relationships and trust.
It encourages young people to prepare and behave well to earn respect. Good conduct opens opportunities to learn from and join elders.

title: Lessons from Things Fall Apart
author: Chinua Achebe · 1958
tag: Africa's most read novel is a study of strength, fear, change and dignity.
ideas: Fear disguised as strength

Okonkwo, the hero of Umuofia, is admired for his strength and achievements. Achebe shows that beneath it lies a fear of being seen as weak like his father, Unoka. Much of his harshness is driven by that fear. Strength rooted in fear eventually breaks.
Rigidity cannot survive change
When missionaries and colonial government arrive, Okonkwo responds only with force. He cannot adapt. Achebe shows that unbending strength, however impressive, can be destroyed by a changing world.
The questioner sees further

Okonkwo's friend Obierika is a thoughtful man who asks why customs are as they are. He is not weaker for questioning; he is wiser. Reflection allows a person to keep what is good and question what is harmful.
A community holds itself in balance

Umuofia has elders, councils, customs and ways of resolving disputes. Achebe shows a complex society with its own justice and wisdom, answering the colonial claim that Africa had no history worth telling.
Telling your own story
Achebe wrote partly in response to European novels that portrayed Africa without dignity. Things Fall Apart insists that a people must tell their own story, or others will tell it wrongly.
When the centre cannot hold

The title, from a poem by W. B. Yeats, describes what happens when the forces holding a community together weaken. Achebe shows that a society can fall apart not only from outside pressure but from internal divisions that outsiders exploit.
faith: And do not be like she who untwisted her spun thread after it was strong. The Qur'an warns against undoing, through broken commitments and division, what has been carefully built. Achebe's novel is a portrait of a society's thread being untwisted. Its lessons for Nigerian leaders today are clear: build unity, adapt wisely without losing your values, and let strength come from faith rather than fear.
practices: Ask yourself honestly where fear is driving your harshness.
Identify one tradition in your work or family that needs questioning, and one that must be protected.
Read or reread Things Fall Apart, and discuss it with your children when they are older.
reflect: Am I adapting to change, or only resisting it?
What keeps the centre holding in my family and organisation?
closing: Strength rooted in fear breaks; wisdom that adapts endures. Tell your own story, and guard what holds you together.

verses.ar: وَلَا تَكُونُوا۟ كَٱلَّتِى نَقَضَتْ غَزْلَهَا مِنۢ بَعْدِ قُوَّةٍ أَنكَٰثًا تَتَّخِذُونَ أَيْمَٰنَكُمْ دَخَلًۢا بَيْنَكُمْ أَن تَكُونَ أُمَّةٌ هِىَ أَرْبَىٰ مِنْ أُمَّةٍ إِنَّمَا يَبْلُوكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِهِۦ وَلَيُبَيِّنَنَّ لَكُمْ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ مَا كُنتُمْ فِيهِ تَخْتَلِفُونَ
verses.en: And do not be like she who untwisted her spun thread after it was strong [by] taking your oaths as [means of] deceit between you because one community is more plentiful [in number or wealth] than another community. Allāh only tries you thereby. And He will surely make clear to you on the Day of Resurrection that over which you used to differ.

deep: Okonkwo's fear of being seen as weak like his father drives him to harshness and violence. Achebe shows how unexamined fear can distort strength and lead to tragedy.
Okonkwo's rigid resistance to change contrasts with others who adapt. Achebe suggests that adaptability, while preserving core values, is necessary for survival in changing times.
Obierika questions traditions thoughtfully, showing that reflection and dialogue can lead to wisdom. His approach balances respect for culture with openness to change.
Achebe depicts Umuofia as a complex society with its own justice systems and values. This challenges colonial narratives that portrayed African societies as primitive.
Achebe wrote to correct misrepresentations of Africa in European literature. His work encourages Africans to tell their own stories with dignity and authenticity.
The title, taken from Yeats's poem The Second Coming, reflects the collapse of a society under internal and external pressures. It warns of the importance of maintaining unity and core values.

title: Long Walk to Freedom
author: Nelson Mandela · 1994
tag: Twenty-seven years in prison, and the leadership lessons that came out of them.
ideas: Prison as a university

On Robben Island, Mandela and his fellow prisoners studied, debated and taught each other. They turned confinement into education, so that the prison became known as a kind of university. Circumstances can limit the body without imprisoning the mind.
Understand your opponent

Mandela learned Afrikaans and studied the history of the Afrikaner people who imprisoned him. Understanding his opponents' fears and pride helped him negotiate with them later. You cannot persuade people you do not understand.
Courage is mastering fear
Mandela wrote that he learned courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it. He admitted feeling afraid many times, and chose to act bravely anyway.
Lead from behind

He compared a leader to a shepherd who stays behind the flock, letting the most nimble go ahead while the others follow, not realising they are being directed from behind. Good leaders often guide quietly and give credit to others.
Reconciliation as strength
After his release, Mandela chose reconciliation over revenge, believing it was the only path to a united nation. Forgiveness was not weakness; it was strategy and principle together.
The walk never ends
He ended his book by reflecting that after climbing one great hill, one finds there are many more hills to climb. Freedom brings new responsibilities, and the walk continues.
faith: And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation, his reward is with Allah. Islam permits just recompense but honours forgiveness above it. When the Prophet, peace be upon him, entered Makkah in victory, he pardoned the people who had persecuted him for years. Mandela's path of reconciliation reflects this prophetic choice: mercy from a position of strength.
practices: Learn something about the perspective of someone you strongly disagree with.
Give credit publicly to a team member for something you guided quietly.
Choose one grievance to forgive this month, for the sake of Allah.
reflect: How can my current constraints become a 'university'?
Where would reconciliation serve better than winning?
closing: Master your fear, understand your opponent, lead from behind, and remember: whoever pardons, his reward is with Allah.

verses.ar: وَجَزَٰٓؤُا۟ سَيِّئَةٍ سَيِّئَةٌ مِّثْلُهَا فَمَنْ عَفَا وَأَصْلَحَ فَأَجْرُهُۥ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
verses.en: And the retribution for an evil act is an evil one like it, but whoever pardons and makes reconciliation - his reward is [due] from Allāh. Indeed, He does not like wrongdoers.

deep: Mandela and his fellow prisoners turned Robben Island into a place of learning, sharing knowledge and debating ideas. This shows how adversity can become an opportunity for growth.
Learning Afrikaans and understanding Afrikaner history helped Mandela build trust with his opponents. It shows the value of understanding others' perspectives in negotiation.
Mandela admitted feeling fear but chose to act bravely. His example shows that courage involves facing fear rather than lacking it.
Mandela's shepherd image describes leadership that empowers others and guides quietly. It reflects humility and trust in the team.
Mandela chose reconciliation to build a united nation. His approach shows that forgiveness can be a powerful tool for peace and progress.
Mandela reflected that achieving freedom brought new responsibilities. Leadership and growth are continuous journeys rather than final destinations.

title: Kaizen: The Toyota Way
author: Taiichi Ohno · Toyota Production System, 1978
tag: How a Japanese carmaker, short of money and space after the war, built a system of daily improvement that the whole world now studies.
ideas: Ask why five times

Taiichi Ohno taught his engineers to ask 'why?' again and again until the real cause appeared. In his book's example, a machine stops because a fuse blew; it blew because a bearing was not lubricated; the pump was not pumping; its shaft was worn; there was no strainer, so metal scraps got in. Fit a strainer, and the problem stops for good, instead of replacing the fuse forever.
Go and see for yourself

Toyota calls it genchi genbutsu: go to the real place and see the real thing. Ohno was known for drawing a chalk circle on the factory floor and asking a young manager to stand in it for hours, simply watching, until he saw the waste no report would ever show. Decisions made only from an office are made half-blind.
Hunt the seven wastes

Ohno named the enemy muda, waste: making too much, waiting, needless transport, over-processing, excess stock, unnecessary motion and defects. None of these add value for the customer, yet every organisation is full of them. Naming waste precisely makes it visible, and what is visible can be removed.
Stop the line when something is wrong

The idea began with Sakichi Toyoda's loom, which stopped by itself when a thread broke so that no faulty cloth was woven. Toyota extended it to people: any worker may stop the production line when they find a defect. Problems are fixed at the source, while they are small, rather than passed down the line to the customer.
Just in time

Ohno took inspiration from American supermarkets, where shelves are refilled only as customers take goods. Toyota makes only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed. Large piles of stock hide problems and tie up money; a lean flow exposes problems quickly so they can be solved.
Small improvements, every day, by everyone

Kaizen means continuous improvement. It does not wait for a grand plan or a genius; it asks every person to make their own work a little better, every day, starting from a written standard. Ohno held that where there is no standard there can be no improvement, because you cannot improve what you have not defined.
faith: Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves. Change begins inside, with honest attention to what is wrong. Kaizen is a disciplined form of this: small, steady changes in how we work. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the deeds most beloved to Allah are the most consistent, even if small, and that Allah loves a person who perfects their work.
hadith: The most beloved of deeds to Allah are those done most consistently, even if they are small.
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464; Sahih Muslim 783
Allah loves that when one of you does a piece of work, he does it with excellence (itqan).
Al-Bayhaqi, Shu'ab al-Iman; graded hasan by al-Albani
practices: Take one recurring problem at work and ask 'why?' five times. Write down the root cause.
Spend thirty minutes simply observing where the real work happens, without interrupting.
Write a one-page standard for one task you repeat, then improve one step of it.
reflect: Which problem am I fixing again and again instead of removing its cause?
Where would I stop the line if I had the courage?
closing: Excellence is not a leap but a habit: small improvements, made every day, by everyone. That is kaizen, and it is also ihsan.

verses.ar: لَهُۥ مُعَقِّبَٰتٌ مِّنۢ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِۦ يَحْفَظُونَهُۥ مِنْ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا۟ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ وَإِذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍ سُوٓءًا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُۥ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِن وَالٍ
verses.en: For him [i.e., each one] are successive [angels] before and behind him who protect him by the decree of Allāh. Indeed, Allāh will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allāh intends for a people ill, there is no repelling it. And there is not for them besides Him any patron.

deep: The five whys work best on the shop floor of any organisation: a delayed payment, a repeated customer complaint, a compliance breach. Stop at the cause you can actually fix, and write it down. If the answer is 'human error', ask why the process allowed the error.

Reports filter reality. Visiting the branch, the site or the customer's office shows you queues, workarounds and frustrations that never reach a dashboard. Leaders who go and see also signal respect for the people doing the work.

Try naming the seven wastes in an office: duplicate approvals (over-processing), files waiting for a signature (waiting), reports nobody reads (overproduction), searching for documents (motion), errors that need rework (defects).

In an office, 'stopping the line' means giving any staff member the right to pause a transaction that looks wrong without fear of blame. Organisations that punish people for raising problems guarantee that problems travel further and grow larger.

Just in time is not only about stock. Information can also be pushed out too early in large batches, or held back until it is stale. Aim for the right information reaching the right person when they need it.

Improvement needs a baseline. Document how a task is done now, measure it, change one thing and measure again. Small, written, tested improvements accumulate into excellence, the practical meaning of itqan.

title: A Compass to Fulfillment
author: Kazuo Inamori · Kyocera, KDDI and Japan Airlines
tag: The engineer-founder who built two global companies and, at 78, rescued Japan's national airline without pay, by asking one question: what is the right thing to do as a human being?
ideas: Result = Way of thinking × Effort × Ability

Inamori summed up his philosophy in one equation. Ability and effort each score from zero to a hundred, but way of thinking runs from minus a hundred to plus a hundred. Because the factors multiply, a talented, hard-working person with a negative or selfish outlook produces a negative result. Character is not a soft extra; it decides the sign of everything else.
Ask what is right as a human being

When Inamori founded Kyocera in 1959 he had no business training. So he chose a simple test for every decision: what is the right thing to do as a human being? Not what is profitable, convenient or customary, but what is fair, honest and kind. He found that this plain question settled many questions that cleverness could not.
Check your motive before a big move

Before entering Japan's newly opened telecom market in 1984, Inamori asked himself night after night whether his motive was virtuous and free of selfish desire. Only when he was satisfied did he found DDI, which grew into KDDI. A big venture tests intentions; examining them first protects you from ambition dressed as service.
Amoeba management: make everyone an owner

Inamori divided Kyocera into small units, 'amoebas', each run like a small business with its own simple accounts, tracking value added per hour of work. Ordinary staff could see how their choices affected results. When people understand the numbers and share responsibility, they think and act like owners rather than spectators.
Work as a way to polish the soul

Inamori taught that throwing yourself fully into your daily work, even dull work, refines character. Diligence teaches patience, humility and gratitude. Work is not only a way to earn money; it is a training ground for the soul, and the quality of our work reflects the quality of our inner life.
Rescuing Japan Airlines

In 2010 JAL went bankrupt with the largest debt of any Japanese company since the war. At 78, Inamori agreed to lead it, unpaid. He taught managers his philosophy and amoeba accounting, and pushed every unit to own its costs. Alongside deep restructuring and state support, JAL returned to strong profit and was relisted in 2012, about two years and seven months after its collapse.
faith: Seek, through what Allah has given you, the home of the Hereafter, but do not forget your share of this world; do good as Allah has done good to you, and do not seek corruption in the land. The verse joins worldly success to moral purpose, which is the heart of Inamori's teaching. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that actions are judged by intentions, which echoes Inamori's habit of testing his motives before acting.
hadith: Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what they intended.
Sahih al-Bukhari 1; Sahih Muslim 1907
practices: Before one decision this week, ask: what is the right thing to do as a human being?
Write down your honest motive for a goal you are chasing. Is it free of selfishness?
Share the key numbers of your team's work with the team, so everyone can act like an owner.
reflect: Where is my way of thinking turning my effort and ability into a negative result?
What would change if I treated my work as a way to polish my soul?
closing: Ability and effort matter, but the way you think decides the direction of both. Keep your motive clean and your work sincere.

verses.ar: وَٱبْتَغِ فِيمَآ ءَاتَىٰكَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلدَّارَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةَ وَلَا تَنسَ نَصِيبَكَ مِنَ ٱلدُّنْيَا وَأَحْسِن كَمَآ أَحْسَنَ ٱللَّهُ إِلَيْكَ وَلَا تَبْغِ ٱلْفَسَادَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُفْسِدِينَ
verses.en: But seek, through that which Allāh has given you, the home of the Hereafter; and [yet], do not forget your share of the world. And do good as Allāh has done good to you. And desire not corruption in the land. Indeed, Allāh does not like corrupters."

deep: The equation explains why some brilliant people fail and some average people succeed. A positive, honest, grateful way of thinking multiplies modest talent; arrogance, cynicism or greed can cancel great talent entirely.

This question cuts through complexity in compliance and leadership. When rules are silent or interests conflict, asking what is fair and honest as a human being, and as a Muslim before Allah, often gives a clearer answer than any policy manual.

Inamori reportedly asked himself 'Is my motive good, without selfish intent?' for months. Muslims will recognise this as muhasabah of the intention. Big decisions deserve examined intentions, because ambition easily disguises itself as service.

Amoeba units work because the numbers are simple, frequent and owned by the people who produce them. Even in a small firm, showing each team its own costs and contribution can change behaviour faster than any lecture.

This idea is close to the Islamic view of work as worship when done with sincerity and excellence. Patience with a difficult client or a tedious task becomes a means of refining character, not just a burden to endure.

The JAL story shows philosophy and numbers working together. Inamori taught values, but he also made every unit measure its costs daily. Culture without accounting drifts; accounting without culture becomes cold. Both were needed.

title: The Book of Five Rings
author: Miyamoto Musashi · Go Rin no Sho, 1645
tag: Japan's most famous swordsman wrote his book of strategy near the end of his life, in a cave, and ended it with nine principles for mastery that apply far beyond the sword.
ideas: The way is in training

Musashi said mastery comes from training, not talk. He described forging over a thousand days and polishing over ten thousand. Skill that will not fail you under pressure is built through long, patient repetition, long after the novelty has gone.
Do nothing which is of no use

The last of Musashi's nine principles is the simplest and the hardest. Every useless movement in a fight is an opening for the opponent. In life, every useless activity steals time and focus from what matters. A master is defined as much by what he does not do.
Pay attention even to small things

Musashi warned that battles are lost through details others ignore: footing, distance, timing, the light. A strategist notices small things early, before they become large. In work, small errors in records, words or promises often grow into big failures.
Perceive what cannot be seen

He distinguished two kinds of looking: a narrow 'seeing' of surface details, and a broad 'perceiving' of the whole situation, including what is not obvious. Look past the opponent's sword to his intention. In leadership, look past the presented report to the real situation behind it.
Know the ways of all professions

Musashi urged warriors to study other crafts: the carpenter's, the merchant's, the scholar's. Each teaches principles that apply elsewhere. Wide learning protects against narrow thinking, and the best ideas often come from outside your own field.
Have no fixed stance

He taught 'attitude, no attitude': guards and stances exist, but you must not cling to any of them. Rigid habits make you predictable and slow. Hold your methods lightly, and adapt to the situation in front of you rather than the one you prepared for.
faith: As for those who strive in Our cause, We will surely guide them to Our ways, and Allah is with those who do good. Striving, mujahadah, is the Qur'anic word for the patient, daily effort that brings guidance and mastery. Musashi's 'nothing which is of no use' closely mirrors a famous hadith: part of the excellence of a person's Islam is leaving what does not concern him.
hadith: Part of the excellence of a person's Islam is that he leaves what does not concern him.
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2317 (hasan); Forty Hadith of al-Nawawi, 12
practices: Choose one skill and train it daily for fifteen minutes this week, without skipping.
List three things you did this week that were of no use. Drop one.
Learn one principle from a profession different from yours and apply it.
reflect: Which habit of mine is a 'fixed stance' I should let go of?
What small detail have I been ignoring that could cost me later?
closing: Train patiently, notice the small, drop the useless and stay flexible. Mastery is the reward of steady striving.

verses.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ جَٰهَدُوا۟ فِينَا لَنَهْدِيَنَّهُمْ سُبُلَنَا وَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَمَعَ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ
verses.en: And those who strive for Us - We will surely guide them to Our ways. And indeed, Allāh is with the doers of good.

deep: Mastery in any field, recitation of the Qur'an, writing, negotiation, analysis, follows the same law: deliberate practice over long periods. Talent opens the door; daily training carries you through it.

Busyness can feel like productivity. Ask of each meeting, message and habit: does this serve a real purpose? The Sunnah teaches the same economy, leaving what does not concern us to make room for what does.
Compliance work is largely the discipline of small things: a missing signature, an expired document, an unreconciled figure. Musashi's warriors would have made excellent auditors.

Perceiving the whole means asking what is not being said: who benefits, what pressure lies behind a request, what pattern links several small incidents. It is the difference between reading a report and understanding a situation.
Cross-training builds judgement. A compliance officer who understands sales, or an engineer who understands finance, sees risks and opportunities that specialists miss.
Flexibility is not the absence of principle. Hold your values firmly and your methods lightly. The goal stays fixed; the route adapts to the terrain.

title: The Art of War
author: Sun Tzu · c. 5th century BCE
tag: The world's oldest surviving book on strategy is less about fighting than about avoiding needless battles, preparing thoroughly and winning wisely.
ideas: Weigh the five factors before you act

Sun Tzu opens with calculation. Before any campaign, compare five things: the moral unity between leader and people, the season and conditions, the ground, the commander's qualities, and organisation and discipline. Many plans fail not in execution but because nobody honestly weighed these first.
Know the other side and know yourself

His most quoted line: if you know the enemy and know yourself, you need not fear the result of a hundred battles. If you know yourself but not the enemy, for every victory you will also suffer a defeat. Know neither, and you will lose every time. Self-knowledge without understanding the other party is only half of wisdom.
The best victory needs no battle

Sun Tzu held that supreme excellence is to break the enemy's resistance without fighting. Fighting is costly even when you win. In negotiations, competition and family disputes, the wisest outcome is often reached through preparation, alliances and persuasion, without open conflict.
Win first, then fight

Victorious warriors win first and then go to war, he wrote, while defeated warriors go to war first and then seek to win. Success is decided largely by preparation: by securing your position, your resources and your information before the decisive moment arrives.
Be like water

Water has no constant shape; it takes its course from the ground it flows over. So an army should shape its plan to the situation, avoiding strength and striking at weakness. A strategy that cannot adapt to changing conditions is a strategy waiting to fail.
Long conflicts drain everyone

Sun Tzu warned that no country has ever benefited from prolonged warfare. Long campaigns exhaust money, morale and people. In business and in life, a quarrel or project that drags on without end often costs more than any victory could repay.
faith: And if they incline to peace, then incline to it also, and rely upon Allah. Islam does not glorify conflict: strength and preparation exist to protect, and peace is preferred whenever it is genuinely available. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told his companions not to wish to meet the enemy but to ask Allah for well-being, and to stand firm if battle came.
hadith: Do not wish to meet the enemy, and ask Allah for well-being; but when you meet them, be patient and stand firm.
Sahih al-Bukhari 3024; Sahih Muslim 1742
practices: Before your next negotiation, write what you know about the other side's interests and your own weaknesses.
Identify one conflict you could resolve without a fight, and take a first step.
Ask of one long-running dispute: what is it really costing us?
reflect: Do I know the other side as well as I know myself?
Which battle am I fighting that wise preparation would make unnecessary?
closing: Prepare thoroughly, understand deeply, prefer peace and adapt like water. The wisest strategist wins before the battle begins.

verses.ar: وَإِن جَنَحُوا۟ لِلسَّلْمِ فَٱجْنَحْ لَهَا وَتَوَكَّلْ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلسَّمِيعُ ٱلْعَلِيمُ
verses.en: And if they incline to peace, then incline to it [also] and rely upon Allāh. Indeed, it is He who is the Hearing, the Knowing.

deep: These five factors can frame any major decision: Do our people believe in this? Is the timing right? Do we understand the terrain? Do we have the right leader? Are we organised and disciplined enough?
In a negotiation, know your own limits, needs and weaknesses as honestly as you study the other party's. Many deals fail because one side overestimated its own position.

The Prophet's treaty of Hudaybiyyah is a profound example: an agreement that seemed like a concession opened the way to peaceful growth and, within two years, the opening of Makkah with little bloodshed.
Preparation is a form of tawakkul when combined with trust in Allah. Gather information, secure resources and plan thoroughly, then rely on Allah for the outcome.
Adapting like water means watching the situation continuously: markets, regulators, competitors and your own team. Rigid plans break; adaptable plans bend and continue.
Count the full cost of a dispute: money, time, relationships, reputation and peace of mind. Often an early fair settlement is worth more than a late victory.

title: The Analects
author: Confucius · 5th century BCE
tag: The sayings of China's great teacher, gathered by his students, shaped East Asian ideas of character, learning and good government for over two thousand years.
ideas: The noble person and the petty person

Confucius contrasted the junzi, the person of noble character, with the petty person. The noble person thinks first of what is right; the petty person thinks first of what profits him. The difference is not wealth or rank but what you reach for when no one is checking.
Do not do to others what you would not want done to you

Asked for one word to guide a whole life, Confucius answered: reciprocity. What you do not want for yourself, do not impose on others. It is a simple rule that, honestly applied, would transform workplaces, markets and homes.
Learn from everyone

When you meet a worthy person, think of becoming their equal; when you meet an unworthy one, look within and examine yourself. Every encounter teaches something: good examples show us what to become, and bad ones show us what to correct in ourselves.
Examine yourself daily

His disciple Zengzi said he examined himself three times a day: Was I loyal in working for others? Was I trustworthy with friends? Did I practise what I was taught? A short daily review is one of the oldest and most effective tools of self-improvement.
Learning and thinking need each other

Confucius said that learning without thinking leads to confusion, and thinking without learning is dangerous. Reading alone does not produce wisdom; neither does clever opinion without study. Real understanding comes when we take in knowledge and then reflect on it seriously.
Call things by their right names

Asked what he would do first in government, Confucius said he would rectify names: if words do not match reality, speech loses its truth, and nothing can be done well. A loss called a 'temporary adjustment', or a bribe called a 'facilitation fee', corrupts thinking before it corrupts action.
faith: O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do? Most hateful it is to Allah that you say what you do not do. Confucius's teaching that words must match reality, and that the noble person acts as he speaks, meets this verse directly. The Prophet, peace be upon him, also gave the believer's version of reciprocity: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
hadith: None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.
Sahih al-Bukhari 13; Sahih Muslim 45
practices: End each day this week with Zengzi's three questions about loyalty, trust and practice.
Find one place where words at work hide reality. Name it honestly.
Before one decision, ask: would I want this done to me?
reflect: When no one is checking, do I reach first for what is right or what profits me?
Which of my words do not match my deeds?
closing: Character, reciprocity, daily self-examination and honest names: simple teachings that still build good people and good institutions.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لِمَ تَقُولُونَ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ
verses.en: O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?

verses.ar: كَبُرَ مَقْتًا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَن تَقُولُوا۟ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ
verses.en: Greatly hateful in the sight of Allāh is that you say what you do not do.

deep: This distinction is close to the Qur'anic contrast between those who seek the face of Allah and those who seek only worldly gain. Character shows in what we choose when profit and right point in different directions.
The Prophet gave this principle a deeper root: love for your brother what you love for yourself. It moves from merely avoiding harm to actively wishing good for others.
This habit turns every colleague, neighbour and stranger into a teacher. It also guards against arrogance, because others' faults become reminders to check ourselves rather than occasions to judge.
Muslim scholars called this muhasabah, holding yourself to account. Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have said: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account.

Study without reflection fills the memory without forming the mind. Reflection without study produces confident opinions on weak foundations. Pair every reading with a question: what does this mean for how I live and work?
Precise words protect integrity. In compliance and finance especially, honest labels for risks, losses and conflicts of interest are the first defence against deception, including self-deception.

title: From Third World to First
author: Lee Kuan Yew · Singapore, 2000
tag: How a small island with no natural resources, expelled from Malaysia in 1965, became one of the world's richest and least corrupt nations within a generation.
ideas: Clean government is the foundation

Lee made the fight against corruption central from the start. Singapore strengthened its anti-corruption agency and law, so that officials living beyond their means could be required to explain their wealth. Senior officials were paid competitive salaries, so that honesty would not mean poverty. Investors and citizens could trust that rules applied to everyone.
Choose by merit, not connection

Singapore selected and promoted people by ability and performance, offering scholarships to its brightest students in return for years of public service. Lee believed a small country could not afford to waste talent or reward connections. Meritocracy, applied consistently, became a source of both competence and legitimacy.
Make yourself useful to the world

With no hinterland and no resources, Singapore decided to plug into the global economy. When many newly independent countries distrusted foreign companies, Singapore invited multinationals, offering stability, skills and good infrastructure. Lee's lesson: a small player must make itself valuable to bigger players.
A home for every family

Lee believed people with a stake in the country would defend it. The Housing and Development Board built flats on a vast scale and helped families to buy them. Today most Singaporeans live in public housing, and most of those homes are owned by the families in them. Ownership created stability and pride.
Build harmony deliberately

Singapore's Chinese, Malay and Indian communities had seen deadly riots in the 1960s. The government made English the common working language while keeping mother tongues in schools, and later used housing quotas to keep estates mixed rather than separated by race. Unity was treated as something to engineer and protect, not to assume.
Think in decades

Lee planned for the long term: water supply, green spaces, education, defence. In 1967 he launched a tree-planting campaign to make Singapore a 'garden city', believing a clean, green city signalled discipline and attracted investors. Many of his choices paid off only twenty or thirty years later.
faith: Allah commands you to render trusts to those to whom they are due, and when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Public office is an amanah, a trust, and corruption is a betrayal of it. The Prophet, peace be upon him, cursed both the one who gives a bribe and the one who takes it. Singapore's experience shows how much a nation gains when that trust is honoured.
hadith: The curse of Allah is on the one who gives a bribe and the one who takes it.
