Sunan Abi Dawud 3580; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1337 (sahih)
practices: Identify one place in your organisation where connection beats merit. Propose one fix.
Write down one decision you are making that will only pay off in ten years.
Review one process for a temptation to corruption, and add a simple check.
reflect: Nigeria and Singapore both gained independence in the 1960s. What can I do, in my own sphere, to close the gap?
Where am I treating a trust as a privilege?
closing: Clean leadership, merit, long-term thinking and deliberate unity can transform a nation. They can also transform a company, a team or a family.

verses.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكُمْ أَن تُؤَدُّوا۟ ٱلْأَمَٰنَٰتِ إِلَىٰٓ أَهْلِهَا وَإِذَا حَكَمْتُم بَيْنَ ٱلنَّاسِ أَن تَحْكُمُوا۟ بِٱلْعَدْلِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ نِعِمَّا يَعِظُكُم بِهِۦٓ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ سَمِيعًۢا بَصِيرًا
verses.en: Indeed, Allāh commands you to render trusts to whom they are due and when you judge between people to judge with justice. Excellent is that which Allāh instructs you. Indeed, Allāh is ever Hearing and Seeing.

deep: Singapore's approach combined strong laws, an independent investigating agency, fair pay and leaders who were seen to obey the same rules. Corruption falls when it becomes both difficult and shameful.
Meritocracy has its critics, who say it can harden into elitism, but its core lesson holds: institutions decay when positions go to the connected rather than the capable.
Making yourself useful applies to individuals as much as nations. A professional who solves important problems for others will always find opportunity.
Home ownership gave citizens a tangible stake in national success. Leaders anywhere can ask: what would give the people I serve a real, personal stake in the outcome?
Deliberate integration recognised that diversity can be a strength or a fault line. Nigeria's diversity, too, needs institutions and habits that build trust across communities.

Long-term thinking requires patience and consistency across many years. Many Nigerian institutions suffer from policy reversals; a culture of continuity can be built in a company or ministry, one decision at a time.

title: The Seeker After Truth
author: Ibn al-Haytham · Book of Optics, c. 1011–1021
tag: The Basra-born scholar who worked in Cairo and is often called the father of the scientific method: he refused to trust any claim, even from the greatest authorities, without evidence.
ideas: The seeker after truth does not simply trust the ancients

In his Doubts Concerning Ptolemy, Ibn al-Haytham wrote that the seeker after truth is not the one who studies the writings of the ancients and puts his trust in them, but the one who suspects his faith in them and follows argument and demonstration. Respect for great names must never replace evidence.
Make yourself an enemy of what you read

He advised the reader of scientific works to attack them from every side, looking for errors and gaps, as if he were their opponent. This is not disrespect; it is how knowledge improves. Ideas that survive honest challenge become stronger.
Suspect yourself too

Ibn al-Haytham added that the investigator must also suspect himself, so that he does not fall into prejudice or leniency. We are quick to see errors in others and slow to see our own biases. Honest inquiry turns its critical eye inward as well as outward.
Test it: experiment and observe

He relied on i'tibar, controlled testing. He showed with dark rooms, small holes and straight tubes that light travels in straight lines, and he studied how images form in what we now call the camera obscura. Claims were to be checked against careful observation, not settled by argument alone.
Overturning an old belief about sight

Many ancient thinkers believed the eye sends out rays to see. Ibn al-Haytham argued, from evidence such as the pain of looking at the sun and afterimages, that light enters the eye from objects. His Book of Optics was translated into Latin and studied by European scientists for centuries.
Use difficult seasons productively

According to the traditional account, Ibn al-Haytham spent years confined in Cairo under the ruler al-Hakim, and used that time to write. Whatever the exact details, his major work on optics came from that period. Restricted circumstances need not mean a wasted life.
faith: Do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge; indeed hearing, sight and the heart will all be questioned. The Qur'an commands us to verify before we believe or repeat a claim, and it repeatedly invites reflection on the signs in creation. Ibn al-Haytham's method is this verse turned into a discipline. The Prophet, peace be upon him, warned that it is enough of a lie for a person to pass on everything he hears.
hadith: It is enough of a lie for a person to relate everything he hears.
Sahih Muslim, Introduction (5)
practices: Before forwarding any news or claim this week, check its source.
Choose one belief you hold strongly at work and look for the best evidence against it.
Test one assumption with a small, real experiment rather than a debate.
reflect: Which authority do I trust without ever checking?
Where might my own bias be making me lenient?
closing: Respect knowledge, but test it. Suspect your sources, suspect yourself, and let evidence decide.

verses.ar: وَلَا تَقْفُ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلْمٌ إِنَّ ٱلسَّمْعَ وَٱلْبَصَرَ وَٱلْفُؤَادَ كُلُّ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْـُٔولًا
verses.en: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.

deep: This principle does not reject tradition; it asks that every claim be weighed by its evidence. Muslim hadith scholars applied a similar rigour, examining chains and narrators rather than trusting a report because it was famous.
Reviewing a policy or report as if you were its strongest critic is excellent practice for compliance officers and leaders. Find the weaknesses before regulators, competitors or events do.
Self-suspicion is the hardest step. Ask: what would I conclude if the evidence pointed against my interest? Do I check my friends' claims as carefully as my opponents'?
Small experiments often settle questions that long debates cannot. Before rolling out a change across an organisation, test it on a small scale and observe the result honestly.
His work shows that a Muslim scholar, motivated in part by the Qur'anic call to reflect, laid foundations for modern optics. Faith and rigorous inquiry are allies, not enemies.
Confinement, illness, a stalled career or a quiet season can become time for deep work, learning or writing, if we choose to use it.

title: The Conditions of Renaissance
author: Malek Bennabi · Algeria, 1949
tag: An Algerian engineer-thinker asked why the Muslim world had declined and how it could rise again. His answer begins inside people, not with imported products.
ideas: Civilisation = person + soil + time

Bennabi offered a formula: civilisation is produced when people, land and time are combined, with faith acting as the catalyst that binds them together. Every society already has these raw materials. What is missing is the spirit and organisation that turns them into progress.
Colonisability comes before colonisation

His most famous idea: a people is colonised because it has first become colonisable, weakened by inner decay, passivity and disunity. Foreign domination exploits this weakness but did not create it. Real liberation therefore starts with changing ourselves, not only with blaming others.
You cannot import a civilisation

Bennabi criticised the habit of piling up the products of other civilisations, machines, buildings and gadgets, and calling it development. Things can be bought; the culture of work, order and ideas that produced them cannot. Accumulation is not construction.
Dead ideas and deadly ideas

He described 'dead ideas', inherited ones that have lost their life and power, and 'deadly ideas', borrowed ones taken out of their original context that harm the society that adopts them. A healthy society revives its own living principles and borrows wisely.
A world of ideas, not only of things and persons

Bennabi observed that societies can be organised around things, around personalities, or around ideas. A society that worships possessions or heroes is fragile; one driven by shared ideas and principles can outlast any leader and rebuild after loss.
Time is capital

For Bennabi, time was a raw material that the Muslim world was wasting. A little disciplined, useful work every day, multiplied across millions of people, could change a nation. Development is not a gift; it is the sum of ordinary hours used well.
faith: That is because Allah would never change a favour He had bestowed upon a people until they change what is within themselves. Bennabi built his whole project on this principle: outward decline follows inward change, and recovery must begin within. The Prophet, peace be upon him, warned that health and free time are two blessings in which many people are cheated.
hadith: There are two blessings in which many people are cheated: health and free time.
Sahih al-Bukhari 6412
practices: Track how you use your evenings for three days. Reclaim one hour for useful work.
Identify one 'dead idea' in your workplace or family that no longer serves its purpose.
Before buying a tool or system, ask whether the habits to use it well exist yet.
reflect: Where in my life have I become 'colonisable' through my own weaknesses?
Is my organisation driven by ideas, by personalities or by things?
closing: Renaissance is not imported; it is built from people, land and time, joined by faith and disciplined work, starting within ourselves.

verses.ar: ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَمْ يَكُ مُغَيِّرًا نِّعْمَةً أَنْعَمَهَا عَلَىٰ قَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا۟ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ وَأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ
verses.en: That is because Allāh would not change a favor which He had bestowed upon a people until they change what is within themselves. And indeed, Allāh is Hearing and Knowing.

deep: The formula reminds us that resources are rarely the real constraint. Nigeria has people, land and time in abundance; what decides the outcome is the faith, values and organisation that bind them.
This is not blaming the victim; Bennabi opposed colonialism fiercely. It is a call to responsibility: the part of the problem within our control is the part we must change first.
Organisations make the same mistake: buying software, buildings and consultants without building the habits of discipline, accuracy and accountability needed to use them.
Ask which inherited practices in your community or company have lost their purpose, and which imported ideas fit poorly with your values and context.
A team built around one strong personality often collapses when that person leaves. A team built around clear principles and shared ideas can survive and grow.
Time is the one resource distributed equally. Bennabi's point is practical: development is the sum of ordinary hours used well, by many people, consistently.

title: The Arthashastra
author: Kautilya (Chanakya) · ancient India
tag: An ancient Indian manual of statecraft that treats government as a serious craft: welfare, finance, intelligence and, strikingly, the many ways officials steal.
ideas: The ruler's happiness lies in the people's happiness

Kautilya wrote that in the happiness of his subjects lies the king's happiness, and in their welfare his welfare. What pleases the ruler personally is not good; what pleases his people is. Leadership is measured by the wellbeing of those you lead.
Stay accessible

He warned that a ruler who makes himself hard to reach, and leaves petitioners waiting at the door, causes confusion and loses the affection of the people. He even proposed a disciplined daily timetable, dividing day and night into parts for hearing people, reviewing finances, consulting and rest.
Officials will be tempted, so design controls

Kautilya observed that just as it is impossible not to taste honey or poison placed on the tongue, it is hard for an official handling revenue not to taste some of it; and just as one cannot tell when a fish swimming in water drinks, it is hard to detect an official's theft. So he designed checks: audits, rotation and supervision.
Know the ways money disappears

The text lists some forty ways of embezzlement, from delaying collections and misrecording dates to inflating costs and substituting goods. Naming the methods precisely is the first step to preventing them. Every good compliance function begins with a clear map of how things go wrong.
Test integrity before you trust

Kautilya described testing ministers' character before appointing them to sensitive posts: their honesty with money, their loyalty and their steadiness under fear or temptation. Positions of trust should be filled by people whose integrity has been observed, not merely assumed.
All undertakings depend on the treasury

He insisted that every undertaking of the state depends first on its finances, so the treasury must be guarded carefully and revenue collected fairly. A leader who ignores the numbers will soon find that nothing else can be done.
faith: Do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor offer it to authorities to devour a portion of people's wealth sinfully while you know. The Qur'an condemns the corruption Kautilya mapped so carefully. The Prophet, peace be upon him, held his own appointed collector to account when he kept 'gifts' received in office, asking why he did not sit in his parents' house to see whether gifts would come to him there.
hadith: Why does he not sit in the house of his father or mother and see whether gifts are given to him or not?
Sahih al-Bukhari 6979; Sahih Muslim 1832
practices: List five ways money could leak from a process you oversee, and one control for each.
Review your gifts and hospitality rules against the Prophet's test: would this gift come if I did not hold this post?
Block time this week to be accessible to people who need your decisions.
reflect: Which honey sits on my tongue in my role?
Do the people I lead feel their welfare is my measure of success?
closing: Serve the people's welfare, stay accessible, guard the treasury and design for human weakness. Good governance is a craft.

verses.ar: وَلَا تَأْكُلُوٓا۟ أَمْوَٰلَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ وَتُدْلُوا۟ بِهَآ إِلَى ٱلْحُكَّامِ لِتَأْكُلُوا۟ فَرِيقًا مِّنْ أَمْوَٰلِ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلْإِثْمِ وَأَنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ
verses.en: And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly or send it [in bribery] to the rulers in order that [they might aid] you [to] consume a portion of the wealth of the people in sin, while you know [it is unlawful].

deep: Islamic political thought makes the same point: the ruler is a servant of the people's welfare. Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported to have feared being asked about a mule stumbling on a road in Iraq.
Accessibility is a form of accountability. Leaders who cannot be reached do not hear bad news until it is too late.

Modern controls such as segregation of duties, job rotation, mandatory leave and surprise audits apply exactly this insight: assume temptation exists, and design so that wrongdoing is hard and quickly detected.
A compliance officer can build a 'ways money disappears' register for each process, with a control and an owner for each risk. Naming the method is half of prevention.
Today this is called due diligence and fit-and-proper testing. Regulators require it for key roles because character, not only competence, determines how power is used.
Financial discipline is a moral duty for anyone entrusted with others' money, including fund managers, treasurers and heads of households.

title: Wings of Fire
author: A. P. J. Abdul Kalam · 1999
tag: The boat owner's son from Rameswaram who sold newspapers as a boy, led India's space and missile programmes, and became the 'People's President', told his story to inspire the young.
ideas: A teacher on the seashore

Kalam recalled a schoolteacher, Sivasubramania Iyer, who explained how birds fly and then took the class to the seashore to watch them. That lesson set the direction of his life towards flight and aeronautics. One good teacher, explaining one thing well, can change a life.
Ninth, when there were eight places

After studying aeronautical engineering, Kalam's dearest dream was to be a fighter pilot. At the Air Force selection in Dehradun he finished ninth when only eight officers were chosen. Deeply disappointed, he accepted it and took the other path open to him, which led to rockets. Failure redirected rather than ended his story.
A leader who takes the blame and gives the credit

In 1979 India's first satellite launch vehicle, SLV-3, which Kalam led, failed. His chief, Professor Satish Dhawan, faced the press and took responsibility himself. When the launch succeeded in 1980, Dhawan sent Kalam to announce it. Kalam said he learned there what leadership means.
Dream, then act

Kalam often told students that dreams become thoughts and thoughts become action. He did not mean daydreams; he meant clear goals that keep you awake and working. A dream is the beginning of a plan, and a plan becomes real only through disciplined effort.
Build teams that build themselves

Kalam's projects relied on large teams of young engineers. He gave them responsibility early, trusted them to solve problems and defended them when things went wrong. Many of his colleagues later led programmes of their own. A leader's legacy is measured by the leaders he leaves behind.
Serve to the last

As President from 2002 to 2007, Kalam kept his simple habits and spoke to millions of students. He died in 2015 doing what he loved, collapsing while giving a lecture at a management institute. A life spent serving and teaching does not retire.
faith: For indeed, with hardship comes ease; indeed, with hardship comes ease. Kalam's life is a long illustration of this promise: poverty, a lost dream and a public failure each opened a door. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught the strong believer to strive for what benefits him, seek Allah's help and not give up, and not to dwell on 'if only' when something goes wrong.
hadith: Strive for what benefits you, seek help from Allah and do not feel helpless. If something befalls you, do not say 'if only I had done such and such', but say: Allah decreed and did as He willed.
Sahih Muslim 2664
practices: Write down one 'ninth place' disappointment and what it redirected you towards.
The next time your team fails, take the blame publicly; when it succeeds, let them present it.
Turn one dream into a written plan with a first step for this week.
reflect: Who was the teacher who changed my direction, and have I thanked them?
Which young person could I give real responsibility to now?
closing: Dream clearly, accept setbacks, take the blame and share the credit. With every hardship comes ease.

verses.ar: فَإِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا
verses.en: For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease [i.e., relief].

verses.ar: إِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا
verses.en: Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.

deep: Every leader can be that teacher: explain one thing clearly, show it rather than only tell it, and spark curiosity in a young person.
Disappointment is information, not a verdict. The door that closes often protects us from a path that was not ours, and points to one that is.
This is perhaps the most quoted leadership lesson from Kalam's life. Taking responsibility for failure protects the team's courage; giving away credit builds its confidence.
Kalam's dreams were tied to hard work and service to his country. Write the dream down, break it into steps and begin the first step today.
Delegating real responsibility, with support, is how organisations grow future leaders. Hoarding responsibility keeps a leader busy and a team small.
Kalam's simplicity in high office, and his devotion to students, show that position is a means of service, not a reward to be enjoyed.

title: Development as Freedom
author: Amartya Sen · 1999
tag: The Nobel economist who saw a famine as a boy argued that development means expanding what people are truly able to do and be, not only raising incomes.
ideas: Development means expanding freedoms

Sen argued that the purpose of development is to enlarge the real freedoms people enjoy: to be healthy, educated, safe, able to work and to take part in community life. Growth in income matters because of what it allows people to do, not as an end in itself.
Look at what people can do and be

He called these 'capabilities'. Two people with the same income may have very different lives if one is disabled, sick or excluded. Good policy asks what people are actually able to achieve, not only what they own.
Income can mislead

Sen pointed out that African Americans in the United States, though far richer on average, had lower chances of surviving to old age than people in some poorer places such as the Indian state of Kerala, where health care and education were widely shared. Money alone does not guarantee wellbeing.
Famines are failures of entitlement

Sen witnessed the Bengal famine of 1943 as a child. His research showed that famines often happen without a large fall in total food supply; people starve because they lose the means to buy or grow food, through falling wages or rising prices. Hunger is a problem of access as well as quantity.
Free press and democracy prevent famine

One of his best-known findings is that no major famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a relatively free press. When governments must answer to voters and journalists, they cannot ignore mass starvation. Accountability is a matter of life and death.
Women's agency changes everything

Sen highlighted evidence that women's education, employment and voice in household decisions reduce child mortality and improve family welfare. Empowering women is not only a matter of fairness; it is one of the most powerful levers of development.
faith: Indeed, Allah commands justice, excellence and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing and oppression. The Qur'an measures a society by justice and care for the vulnerable, not by wealth alone. The Prophet, peace be upon him, commanded: feed the hungry, visit the sick and free the captive, practical acts that expand the real freedoms of others.
hadith: Feed the hungry, visit the sick and set free the captive.
Sahih al-Bukhari 5649
practices: Ask of one programme or policy you are involved in: what does it actually allow people to do?
Support the education or work of one woman or girl in your family or community.
Check one source of news this week against a second, independent one.
reflect: Am I measuring success in my family or work by income alone?
Whose real freedom could I expand this month?
closing: True development is measured by what people are free to be and do. Justice, accountability and care make that freedom real.

verses.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَأْمُرُ بِٱلْعَدْلِ وَٱلْإِحْسَٰنِ وَإِيتَآئِ ذِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ وَيَنْهَىٰ عَنِ ٱلْفَحْشَآءِ وَٱلْمُنكَرِ وَٱلْبَغْىِ يَعِظُكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ
verses.en: Indeed, Allāh orders justice and good conduct and giving [help] to relatives and forbids immorality and bad conduct and oppression. He admonishes you that perhaps you will be reminded.

deep: Applied to a company or family, this asks: are the people in my care growing in health, knowledge, skill and dignity, or only producing income?
The capability view is especially useful for policy and philanthropy, because it shows who is being left behind even when averages look good.
Wealth without health care, education and social trust leaves people vulnerable. Nigeria's development debates often focus on GDP; Sen's work asks what life is actually like for ordinary people.
Sen's analysis changed how famine relief works: protecting purchasing power through employment schemes and cash support can save lives as effectively as shipping food.
A free press and open debate are early-warning systems. Organisations, too, need channels where bad news can travel up without fear.
Islam honoured women's education and economic rights from its beginning; Sen's research gives modern evidence for the benefits.

title: Sejong the Great
author: King Sejong · Joseon Korea, reigned 1418–1450
tag: The king who gave Koreans their alphabet, consulted his people on taxes and promoted talent regardless of birth is remembered as a model of learned, caring leadership.
ideas: An alphabet so ordinary people could read

Literary Chinese was hard to learn, so most Koreans could not read or write. Sejong led the creation of a new script, promulgated in 1446 as Hunminjeongeum, 'the correct sounds for instructing the people'. Its preface says he pitied the many who could not express their thoughts, and made letters easy to learn and use daily. That script, Hangul, is still used today.
Ask the people before deciding

Tax assessments were often unfair and open to bribery. In 1430 Sejong had his officials survey opinion on a proposed land tax across the country over about five months, gathering the views of some 170,000 people, from officials to farmers. Because opinions divided, he kept refining the reform for years before settling it in 1444.
Gather the best minds

Sejong expanded the Hall of Worthies, Jiphyeonjeon, a royal institute where talented scholars researched language, history, agriculture, medicine and law. He protected their time for study. Leaders who surround themselves with capable, well-supported thinkers make better decisions.
Promote talent, not only birth

Sejong's chief inventor, Jang Yeong-sil, came from humble origins in a strictly hierarchical society, yet Sejong promoted him for his skill. Jang built water clocks, sundials and instruments; Sejong's reign also produced a standardised rain gauge in 1441 to record rainfall across the provinces. Talent was found and used where it was.
Mercy in the rules

Female slaves working in government offices once received only seven days' leave after giving birth. In 1426 Sejong extended this to 100 days, in 1430 added a month before birth, and in 1434 gave their husbands 30 days to care for them. Even at the bottom of society, rules could be made humane.
Learn from those who do the work

In 1429 Sejong had farming knowledge collected from experienced farmers in the southern provinces and compiled into Nongsa jikseol, 'Straight Talk on Farming', adapted to Korean conditions. Practical wisdom often lies with practitioners, not only with scholars at court.
faith: And those who respond to their Lord and establish prayer, and whose affairs are decided by consultation among themselves. Shura, consultation, is a Qur'anic quality of the believing community. Sejong's polling of his people and support for scholars is a striking example of it. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that each of us is a shepherd responsible for his flock.
hadith: Each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock.
Sahih al-Bukhari 893; Sahih Muslim 1829
practices: Before one decision this week, ask the people it affects for their view.
Find one capable person in a junior role and give them a real opportunity.
Review one policy you control for mercy towards the weakest person it affects.
reflect: Whose voice am I not hearing before I decide?
What could I make easier for ordinary people to understand or use?
closing: Consult your people, gather the best minds, promote talent and make rules humane. That is leadership as service.

verses.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ ٱسْتَجَابُوا۟ لِرَبِّهِمْ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأَمْرُهُمْ شُورَىٰ بَيْنَهُمْ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَٰهُمْ يُنفِقُونَ
verses.en: And those who have responded to their Lord and established prayer and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves, and from what We have provided them, they spend,

deep: Leaders can apply this by making their own communications, policies and forms simple enough for everyone affected to understand.
The tax reform took years because Sejong took objections seriously. Consultation slows decisions down at first but makes them stronger and more legitimate.
Strong leaders are not threatened by capable advisers. Sejong's investment in scholars reflects the Qur'anic command to consult and the Prophet's habit of seeking counsel.
Islam's message of human equality before Allah gives Muslim leaders every reason to look for talent beyond tribe, family and class.
Compassion can be built into policy. Ask who is most vulnerable under a rule and whether a small change could ease their burden.
Experienced staff, farmers, traders and artisans often hold knowledge that leaders lack. Collecting and sharing it is a mark of humble, effective leadership.

title: Saemaul Undong: The New Village Movement
author: South Korea · from 1970
tag: A rural development drive built on three words, diligence, self-help and cooperation, that helped transform Korean villages and is now studied across Africa.
ideas: Three words: diligence, self-help, cooperation

The movement, launched in 1970 under President Park Chung-hee, rested on three values: geunmyeon (diligence), jajo (self-help) and hyeopdong (cooperation). Villagers were asked not to wait for government to do everything, but to work together to improve their own communities.
Give a little, and let people decide

In the first year the government gave each of more than 33,000 villages about 335 bags of cement, free, to use on any shared project the villagers chose: roads, bridges, wells, roofs or laundries. People decided their own priorities and supplied the labour. Ownership of the choice created ownership of the result.
Reward results, not promises

The next year, support went to the villages that had used the cement well. Roughly half, about 16,600 villages, received more cement and steel; villages that had done nothing got no further help. Performance-based support encouraged effort and healthy competition between communities.
Local leaders make the difference

Each village chose a Saemaul leader, often a respected volunteer, and many were trained in leadership and practical skills. The movement found that the quality of local leadership mattered more than the size of the grant.
From roofs to incomes

Early projects improved living conditions: replacing thatched roofs, widening roads, building bridges and bringing water and electricity. Later phases focused on raising incomes through better farming, cooperatives and small rural industries. Visible early wins built confidence for harder work.
A lesson with honest limits

The movement was government-driven, used heavily for political mobilisation and later criticised for top-down control and some misuse of funds, and it did not stop young people leaving for the cities. Its lasting lessons, studied by countries in Africa and Asia, are self-help, local ownership and rewarding performance, applied with accountability.
faith: Cooperate in righteousness and piety, and do not cooperate in sin and aggression. The Qur'an makes cooperation for the common good an act of worship. The Prophet, peace be upon him, described believers as a building whose parts support one another. Communities that work together on shared needs live out this teaching.
hadith: The believer to the believer is like a building, each part strengthening the other.
Sahih al-Bukhari 481; Sahih Muslim 2585
practices: Identify one shared problem in your street, estate or community that neighbours could fix together.
When you support a project, give a little first and add more only when it is used well.
Train or mentor one local volunteer leader.
reflect: What am I waiting for government or others to do that my community could start?
Do I reward results or promises?
closing: Diligence, self-help and cooperation, with honest accountability, can lift a village. They can lift a team or a community too.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لَا تُحِلُّوا۟ شَعَٰٓئِرَ ٱللَّهِ وَلَا ٱلشَّهْرَ ٱلْحَرَامَ وَلَا ٱلْهَدْىَ وَلَا ٱلْقَلَٰٓئِدَ وَلَآ ءَآمِّينَ ٱلْبَيْتَ ٱلْحَرَامَ يَبْتَغُونَ فَضْلًا مِّن رَّبِّهِمْ وَرِضْوَٰنًا وَإِذَا حَلَلْتُمْ فَٱصْطَادُوا۟ وَلَا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ شَنَـَٔانُ قَوْمٍ أَن صَدُّوكُمْ عَنِ ٱلْمَسْجِدِ ٱلْحَرَامِ أَن تَعْتَدُوا۟ وَتَعَاوَنُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلْبِرِّ وَٱلتَّقْوَىٰ وَلَا تَعَاوَنُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلْإِثْمِ وَٱلْعُدْوَٰنِ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ شَدِيدُ ٱلْعِقَابِ
verses.en: O you who have believed, do not violate the rites of Allāh or [the sanctity of] the sacred month or [neglect the marking of] the sacrificial animals and garlanding [them] or [violate the safety of] those coming to the Sacred House seeking bounty from their Lord and [His] approval. But when you come out of iḥrām, then [you may] hunt. And do not let the hatred of a people for having obstructed you from al-Masjid al-Ḥarām lead you to transgress. And cooperate in righteousness and piety, but do not cooperate in sin and aggression. And fear Allāh; indeed, Allāh is severe in penalty.

deep: Each value guards against a failure: diligence against laziness, self-help against dependency and cooperation against division. Together they describe the culture any community needs to develop.
When people choose the project, they protect and maintain it. Many development projects fail because outsiders chose them.
This conditional approach is used today in results-based financing. It requires honest monitoring, or it simply rewards the best storytellers.
Development partners in Africa, including Nigeria, have studied Saemaul training for community leaders. Investing in local leadership is often the highest-return investment.
Visible improvements build belief. Leaders should look for an early, shared, tangible win before asking people for harder, longer-term sacrifices.
Learning honestly from any model means taking its strengths and noting its failures. Self-help and local ownership travel well; top-down pressure and political control do not.

title: The Damascus Sermon
author: Bediuzzaman Said Nursi · 1911
tag: In a sermon at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus, the Turkish scholar diagnosed the illnesses of the Muslim world and prescribed cures that still speak to us.
ideas: Three enemies: ignorance, poverty and disunity

Nursi taught that the greatest enemies of the Muslim world were ignorance, poverty and disunity, and that they must be fought with knowledge, skilled work and unity. Not slogans, not blame, but learning, productive effort and solidarity.
Despair is a deadly disease

Among the illnesses he named, the first was despair, which had entered the hearts of Muslims and killed their energy. He insisted on hope, arguing that the future belonged to truth. Hopelessness, he warned, makes people give up before they begin.
Truthfulness is the foundation

He named the death of truthfulness in social and political life as another illness, and declared truthfulness the foundation of Islam and the bond of society. Lies may seem useful for a time, but a community that tolerates them loses the trust everything else depends on.
Love is most worthy of love

Nursi observed that love of enmity had spread among believers. He taught that the thing most worthy of love is love itself, and the thing most deserving of enmity is enmity itself. Our energy should go into building bonds, not feeding quarrels.
Consultation is the key

He described shura, consultation, as the key to the progress and happiness of the community. Individuals working alone, however gifted, cannot match the combined understanding of many minds working together honestly.
Positive action, even in hardship

Nursi spent decades in exile and prison, yet he kept writing his Risale-i Nur, a commentary on the Qur'an's teachings, which students copied by hand and spread across Turkey. He taught 'positive action': serving faith constructively, without violence or revenge, whatever the circumstances.
faith: Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah; indeed Allah forgives all sins. Nursi's cure for despair rests on this verse: hope is not naivety but faith in Allah's mercy and promise. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that truthfulness leads to righteousness and righteousness leads to Paradise, which Nursi made a pillar of renewal.
hadith: Truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise.
Sahih al-Bukhari 6094; Sahih Muslim 2607
practices: Pick one of the three enemies, ignorance, poverty or disunity, and take one action against it this week.
Replace one complaint with one constructive step.
Bring one decision to honest consultation with your family or team.
reflect: Where has despair quietly reduced my effort?
Am I spending more energy on enmity than on building bonds?
closing: Fight ignorance with knowledge, poverty with work and disunity with love and consultation. Never despair.

verses.ar: قُلْ يَٰعِبَادِىَ ٱلَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا۟ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا۟ مِن رَّحْمَةِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ يَغْفِرُ ٱلذُّنُوبَ جَمِيعًا إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ ٱلْغَفُورُ ٱلرَّحِيمُ
verses.en: Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves [by sinning], do not despair of the mercy of Allāh. Indeed, Allāh forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful."

deep: This diagnosis remains striking for Nigeria and much of the Muslim world. Each of us can contribute to the cure in our own field: teaching, building businesses and bridging divides.
Hope is not wishful thinking; it is the conviction that effort guided by truth will bear fruit, in this life or the next. Despair is a defeat accepted before the contest.
Organisations, too, depend on truthfulness. Once staff believe that reports are dressed up, every number becomes suspect and good decisions become impossible.
This principle is a practical guide in family and workplace disputes: direct your opposition at the behaviour or the enmity itself, not at the person.
Nursi's emphasis on shura echoes the Qur'an's description of believers whose affairs are by consultation. It applies to families, companies and communities alike.
His decades of perseverance show that constructive work can continue under the hardest restrictions. Positive action refuses both despair and violence.

title: The Ahi Brotherhood
author: Ahi Evran and the craft guilds of Anatolia · from the 13th century
tag: Medieval Turkish craftsmen joined faith, skill and business ethics in brotherhoods that trained apprentices, guarded quality and looked after strangers.
ideas: Faith, craft and ethics together

The Ahi brotherhoods grew in thirteenth-century Anatolia, traditionally linked to Ahi Evran, a tanner and scholar of Kırşehir. They organised craftsmen and traders around shared rules of skill and morality, so that a man's work and his faith were judged together.
Master your hand, your tongue and your desires

A well-known Turkish saying associated with this tradition tells a person to be master of his hand, his tongue and his waist: do not take what is not yours, do not speak what harms, and guard your chastity. In business this means honest dealing, careful speech and self-control.
Learn the craft step by step

Young people entered as apprentices, rose to journeymen and only became masters after years of training and proof of skill and character. Advancement was earned. This patient system protected quality and passed on not only techniques but manners.
Quality is a matter of honour

Guilds inspected work and disciplined members who cheated customers or sold faulty goods. Turkish still uses the phrase 'his shoes were thrown on the roof', traditionally explained as the shame of a cheating craftsman expelled from the guild. A trader's reputation was the community's business.
Hospitality to the stranger

The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta, crossing Anatolia in the 1330s, described young Ahi brotherhoods who competed to host travellers, giving them food and lodging generously. Commerce and generosity were not opposites; the same people did both.
Share the market

An old Ottoman marketplace custom, often linked to Ahi ethics, holds that a shopkeeper who has already made his first sale of the day may send a customer to a neighbour who has not. Competition existed, but within a sense of brotherhood that left room for everyone to earn.
faith: Woe to those who give less than due, who, when they take a measure from people, take in full, but when they give by measure or weight, give less. The Qur'an treats honesty in trade as a matter of faith, and the Ahi guilds built that principle into daily commerce. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that whoever cheats is not of us.
hadith: Whoever cheats us is not of us.
Sahih Muslim 102
practices: Check one product or service you deliver for any hidden 'short measure'.
Pass on one skill to a younger person properly, step by step.
Do one generous act for a stranger or a competitor this week.
reflect: Am I master of my hand, my tongue and my desires at work?
Would my trade survive the Ahi inspection?
closing: Skill with ethics, quality as honour, generosity alongside profit: the Ahi way is still a model for Muslim business.

verses.ar: وَيْلٌ لِّلْمُطَفِّفِينَ
verses.en: Woe to those who give less [than due],

verses.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ إِذَا ٱكْتَالُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلنَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ
verses.en: Who, when they take a measure from people, take in full.

verses.ar: وَإِذَا كَالُوهُمْ أَو وَّزَنُوهُمْ يُخْسِرُونَ
verses.en: But if they give by measure or by weight to them, they cause loss.

deep: The model shows that business ethics need institutions as well as individual piety: shared rules, training, inspection and consequences.
This saying is a compact code of conduct for any professional: integrity with money, discipline in speech and control of desires.
Structured apprenticeship builds both skill and character. Modern firms can recreate it through mentoring, clear stages of progression and assessment of conduct as well as output.
A shared reputation encourages everyone to police quality. Professional bodies and industry associations can play this role today.
Generosity to travellers and strangers was part of the brotherhood's identity. Hospitality builds trust, and trust is the foundation of trade.
This custom reflects a view of the market as a community, not a battlefield. Healthy competition and brotherly fairness can coexist.

title: The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam
author: Muhammad Iqbal · 1930
tag: The poet-philosopher of South Asia called Muslims to rediscover the strength of the self, the dynamism of their faith and the courage to think afresh.
ideas: Khudi: develop your self

Iqbal's central idea is khudi, selfhood: a strong, active, responsible self that grows through love, effort and obedience to Allah. He criticised teachings that asked Muslims to dissolve the self into passivity. The believer is meant to be a vigorous agent in the world, not a spectator.
Raise yourself so high

In one of his best-known couplets, Iqbal urged: raise your selfhood so high that before every decree, Allah Himself asks His servant what he wishes. It is poetry, not theology to be taken literally, but its message is clear: through effort and nearness to Allah, a person can shape his destiny rather than merely endure it.
Ijtihad is the principle of movement

In his lectures, Iqbal called ijtihad, independent scholarly reasoning, the principle of movement in Islam. Without it, he argued, Muslim thought freezes while life moves on. Faithful renewal means applying unchanging principles wisely to changing conditions.
The falcon, not the vulture

Iqbal's favourite symbol was the shaheen, the falcon: it flies high, hunts for itself, does not feed on carrion and builds no comfortable nest. He held it up to the young as a picture of dignity, self-reliance and lofty aims.
Learn from the West without losing yourself

Iqbal studied at Cambridge and earned a doctorate in Germany, engaging deeply with Western philosophy. He admired its energy and inquiry but rejected its materialism. His model is critical engagement: take what is true and useful, and remain rooted in your own faith.
Action and hope over lament

Iqbal's poems such as Shikwa and Jawab-e-Shikwa, the Complaint and the Answer, moved from lamenting Muslim decline to answering it: the fault lies with Muslims' own neglect, and the remedy is renewed faith and action. Complaint is not a strategy.
faith: And that there is not for man except that for which he strives, and that his striving is going to be seen, then he will be recompensed with the fullest reward. Iqbal built his philosophy of the self on verses like these: human effort matters and is noticed. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught a man to tie his camel and then rely on Allah, joining action to trust.
hadith: Tie it, and rely upon Allah.
Jami' al-Tirmidhi 2517 (hasan)
practices: Write down one area of life where you have been passive, and one action to take charge of it.
Replace one complaint about the state of things with one thing you will do.
Read one serious idea from outside your tradition and evaluate it in the light of your faith.
reflect: Am I living as a falcon or waiting like a vulture?
Where does my faith call me to think afresh rather than repeat?
closing: Strengthen the self through faith and striving, think with courage, and act with hope. Then rely on Allah.

verses.ar: وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَٰنِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ
verses.en: And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives

verses.ar: وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُۥ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ
verses.en: And that his effort is going to be seen -

verses.ar: ثُمَّ يُجْزَىٰهُ ٱلْجَزَآءَ ٱلْأَوْفَىٰ
verses.en: Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense -

deep: Khudi is not selfishness. It is a strong, purposeful self in the service of Allah and others, the opposite of both arrogance and passivity.
The couplet is often quoted to inspire young people to aim high and work hard, while remembering that every decree remains with Allah. It is a call to effort, not a claim to control.
For Iqbal, renewal means returning to the Qur'an and Sunnah with fresh questions, through qualified scholarship, so that Muslims can respond to modern challenges with confidence.
The falcon also teaches restraint: it refuses easy, dishonourable gains. Dignity sometimes means saying no to comfortable shortcuts.
This balanced approach suits Muslim professionals trained in Western systems: learn deeply, keep what is true and useful, and filter it through Islamic values.
Iqbal's movement from complaint to answer is a model for personal reflection: honestly name the problem, then ask what part of it is mine to fix.

title: Islam and Secularism
author: Syed Muhammad Naquib al-Attas · Malaysia, 1978
tag: The Malaysian philosopher argued that the deepest crisis of Muslims is not poverty or politics but the loss of adab, the right ordering of knowledge, people and things.
ideas: The root problem is the loss of adab

Al-Attas diagnosed the Muslim crisis as a confusion and error in knowledge, which leads to the loss of adab, and in turn to leaders who are not qualified to lead. Fix knowledge and adab, he argued, and much else follows.
What adab really means

For al-Attas, adab is not mere etiquette. It is recognising and acknowledging the proper place of everything: of Allah, of the Prophet, of scholars, of people, of knowledge and of oneself. A person of adab puts things where they belong, which is the essence of justice.
The purpose of education is a good human being

He argued that Islamic education aims to produce a good human being, not merely a good citizen or a skilled worker. Skills matter, but a skilled person without moral and spiritual formation can do great harm.
Ta'dib: education as cultivation

Al-Attas preferred the term ta'dib, instilling adab, to describe Islamic education, because it unites knowledge, character and action. Learning is complete only when it shapes how we behave and how we order our priorities.
The levelling of leaders

He warned against a 'levelling' attitude that refuses to recognise real scholarly and moral authority, treating every opinion as equal. When people cannot tell the learned from the merely loud, unqualified leaders rise.
Not all knowledge is equal

Al-Attas distinguished knowledge that is obligatory for every person, knowledge of faith, worship and character, from specialised knowledge needed by the community. Both are valuable, but neglecting the first while pursuing only the second produces clever people who have lost their way.
faith: And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge. The Prophet, peace be upon him, was commanded to ask for more knowledge, and al-Attas reminds us that knowledge must lead to adab, right conduct and right ordering. The Prophet also said that seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.
hadith: Seeking knowledge is an obligation upon every Muslim.
Sunan Ibn Majah 224; graded sahih by al-Albani
practices: List what you are learning this month. Is any of it the knowledge obligatory for you as a Muslim?
Practise adab in one relationship: give a teacher, parent or elder their due respect.
Before following a voice online, ask whether it has real knowledge and character.
reflect: Have I put knowledge, people and things in their proper place?
Is my learning making me a better human being, or only a more skilled one?
closing: Seek knowledge that leads to adab, and adab that leads to justice. That is the education of a good human being.

verses.ar: فَتَعَٰلَى ٱللَّهُ ٱلْمَلِكُ ٱلْحَقُّ وَلَا تَعْجَلْ بِٱلْقُرْءَانِ مِن قَبْلِ أَن يُقْضَىٰٓ إِلَيْكَ وَحْيُهُۥ وَقُل رَّبِّ زِدْنِى عِلْمًا
verses.en: So high [above all] is Allāh, the Sovereign, the Truth. And, [O Muḥammad], do not hasten with [recitation of] the Qur’ān before its revelation is completed to you, and say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge."

deep: His diagnosis suggests that many visible problems, weak institutions, poor leadership, social division, have a root in confused knowledge and misplaced priorities.
In this sense adab is close to justice, 'adl: giving everything its rightful place. Respecting a teacher, honouring a parent and valuing time are all acts of adab.
Employers notice this too: skills can be taught quickly, but integrity, humility and responsibility are much harder to instil later.
Ta'dib describes the classical Islamic ideal of learning, where scholars were known for their conduct as much as their knowledge.
In the age of social media, the levelling problem is everywhere. Al-Attas's warning encourages us to seek knowledge from people of proven learning and character.
A balanced life of learning includes both: personal religious knowledge for one's own soul, and professional knowledge for serving the community.

title: Atomic Habits
author: James Clear · 2018
tag: Tiny changes, compounded daily, produce remarkable results.
hadith: The most beloved deeds to Allah are those done consistently, even if they are small.
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464, Sahih Muslim 783
ideas: One percent better every day

Clear's starting point is compounding. Improving by just one percent a day makes you dramatically better over a year, while getting one percent worse each day quietly ruins you. Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement: their effects are invisible at first, then sudden and large.
Systems beat goals

Winners and losers often have the same goals. What separates them is the system: the daily process. Clear argues that we should focus less on the target and more on the repeatable actions that move us towards it. A goal is a direction; a system is the road you actually walk.
Change your identity, not just your behaviour

The deepest habits are identity-based. Instead of 'I want to read more', say 'I am a reader'. Every small action is a vote for the type of person you want to become. You do not need a unanimous vote, just a majority.
The four laws of behaviour change

To build a good habit: make it obvious, make it attractive, make it easy, and make it satisfying. To break a bad one, invert the laws: make it invisible, unattractive, difficult and unsatisfying. Most failures come from relying on willpower instead of redesigning these four conditions.
Habit stacking and the two-minute rule

Attach a new habit to an existing one: after I pray Fajr, I will read one page. And scale the start down until it takes two minutes or less. The goal of the first weeks is not performance; it is to become the kind of person who shows up.
Never miss twice
Everyone slips. Clear's rule is simple: missing once is an accident; missing twice is the start of a new habit. When you break the chain, get back the very next day, without guilt or drama.
faith: Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear. This verse removes the excuse that change requires heroic effort. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the most beloved deeds are the consistent ones, even if small. Atomic Habits, read through Islamic eyes, is a modern manual for istiqamah: steadiness on the straight path, one small deed at a time.
practices: Choose one habit and shrink it to a two-minute version you can do daily.
Write one habit stack: 'After [current habit], I will [new habit].'
Remove one trigger from your environment that feeds a bad habit.
reflect: What identity am I voting for with my daily actions?
Which goal of mine lacks a system?
closing: Small, consistent, and steady. Make it easy, make it daily, and never miss twice.

verses.ar: لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا لَهَا مَا كَسَبَتْ وَعَلَيْهَا مَا ٱكْتَسَبَتْ رَبَّنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذْنَآ إِن نَّسِينَآ أَوْ أَخْطَأْنَا رَبَّنَا وَلَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَآ إِصْرًا كَمَا حَمَلْتَهُۥ عَلَى ٱلَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِنَا رَبَّنَا وَلَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِۦ وَٱعْفُ عَنَّا وَٱغْفِرْ لَنَا وَٱرْحَمْنَآ أَنتَ مَوْلَىٰنَا فَٱنصُرْنَا عَلَى ٱلْقَوْمِ ٱلْكَٰفِرِينَ
verses.en: Allāh does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity. It will have [the consequence of] what [good] it has gained, and it will bear [the consequence of] what [evil] it has earned. "Our Lord, do not impose blame upon us if we have forgotten or erred. Our Lord, and lay not upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear. And pardon us; and forgive us; and have mercy upon us. You are our protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people."

deep: Clear illustrates compounding with the British cycling team, whose coach sought tiny improvements in every detail, from bike seats to pillows, until the team began winning repeatedly. The lesson for any professional is that steady, small refinements in your daily work, such as a cleaner report template or a faster review routine, add up to a large edge over years.

Clear notes that goals can even work against you: once reached, the motivation disappears. A system, such as reading ten pages after Fajr or reviewing files for thirty minutes each morning, keeps working long after any single goal is achieved.

He describes three layers of change: outcomes, processes and identity. Most people start with outcomes. Lasting change starts with identity, then lets the processes follow. Islam frames this deeply: the believer acts as a servant of Allah, and small consistent deeds express that identity.

For example, to read Qur'an daily: make it obvious by leaving the mushaf on your pillow; attractive by pairing it with your morning tea; easy by starting with one page; and satisfying by marking a simple tracker. Each law removes a little friction.

Habit stacking uses the stable anchors of daily life. For a Muslim, the five prayers are ideal anchors: after Fajr, a page of Qur'an; after Dhuhr, five minutes of planning; after Isha, a short reflection on the day.

This rule protects identity. One missed day does not change who you are; two in a row starts to. Clear's advice matches the prophetic emphasis on returning quickly after a lapse rather than giving up entirely.

title: Deep Work
author: Cal Newport · 2016
tag: The ability to focus without distraction is becoming rare, and therefore more valuable.
ideas: Deep work versus shallow work

Newport defines deep work as focused effort on a cognitively demanding task, without distraction, that pushes your abilities to their limit. Shallow work is logistical: emails, messages, routine meetings. Shallow work keeps you busy; deep work creates value.
Attention residue

Research by Sophie Leroy shows that when you switch from one task to another, part of your attention stays stuck on the first. Checking messages 'just for a minute' leaves a residue that lowers the quality of your thinking for much longer. Constant switching makes everyone less intelligent.
Choose a depth philosophy

Newport describes four ways to schedule deep work: monastic, cutting out almost all distraction; bimodal, alternating deep days and shallow days; rhythmic, a fixed daily deep block; and journalistic, fitting depth in wherever possible. Most professionals with many duties succeed with the rhythmic approach.
Embrace boredom

If you reach for your phone at every idle moment, your brain loses the ability to sustain focus. Newport recommends scheduling internet use, rather than scheduling breaks from it, so that concentration becomes the default and distraction the exception.
Quit the tools that do not serve your goals

He urges a hard look at social media: keep a tool only if its benefits clearly outweigh its costs for your most important goals. 'It might be useful' is not good enough when the cost is your attention.
End the day with a shutdown ritual
At the end of each workday, review open tasks, plan the next day, and then declare work finished. This ritual lets the mind rest, which is necessary for deep work the following day.
faith: Certainly will the believers have succeeded: they who are during their prayer humbly focused, and they who turn away from vain talk. The Qur'an describes success as beginning with khushu', the deep focus of prayer, and continuing with turning away from laghw, idle and useless speech. Five daily prayers are, among other things, five lessons in single-tasking. A believer trained in khushu' has the foundation of deep work.
practices: Block 90 minutes each morning for one important task, phone in another room.
Batch messages and emails into two or three fixed times a day.
Create a five-minute shutdown ritual at the end of the workday.
reflect: How many minutes of truly undistracted work did I do yesterday?
Which app takes more from me than it gives?
closing: Focus is the new scarcity. Guard it in prayer, guard it at work, and turn away from what is vain.

verses.ar: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ
verses.en: Certainly will the believers have succeeded:

verses.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ فِى صَلَاتِهِمْ خَٰشِعُونَ
verses.en: They who are during their prayer humbly intent

verses.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ عَنِ ٱللَّغْوِ مُعْرِضُونَ
verses.en: And they who turn away from ill speech

deep: Newport argues that deep work is how valuable things get produced: analysis, writing, strategy, learning a difficult skill. Shallow work is necessary, but if it fills the whole day, a person stays busy without producing anything that sets them apart.

Leroy's studies found that people who switched tasks before finishing performed worse on the next task, because their attention was still partly on the first. This is why a quick look at messages before an important meeting can quietly reduce your thinking for the next hour.

For someone managing several roles, the rhythmic approach works well: a fixed daily block, such as 7 to 9 am, reserved for the most demanding thinking. The consistency removes the need to decide each day when deep work will happen.

Newport suggests practising focus like a muscle: wait in a queue without reaching for your phone, or go for a walk while thinking through a single problem. Over time, the mind becomes able to hold attention for longer.

His approach is not to reject all technology, but to judge each tool by whether it substantially serves your core goals. For many professionals, a professional network may pass the test while endless scrolling feeds do not.

Newport's ritual includes reviewing every pending task and making a plan for each, then saying a set phrase to signal the end of work. The point is to close open loops so the mind can genuinely rest with family in the evening.

title: Essentialism
author: Greg McKeown · 2014
tag: Less, but better: the disciplined pursuit of what truly matters.
ideas: Less, but better

McKeown borrows the phrase of the designer Dieter Rams: less, but better. An essentialist does not try to do everything; he identifies the vital few and gives them full energy. Spreading yourself across many things produces a millimetre of progress in a thousand directions.
If you do not prioritise your life, someone else will

When you have no clear priorities, other people's priorities fill your calendar. Every yes to something unimportant is a silent no to something important. Saying no, gracefully and clearly, is a leadership skill.
The 90 percent rule

When deciding whether to take on an opportunity, rate it from zero to a hundred against your most important criteria. If it scores below ninety, treat it as a zero and decline. Clear yeses deserve your energy; maybes rarely do.
Trade-offs are real

Non-essentialists ask, 'How can I do both?' Essentialists ask, 'Which problem do I want?' Every choice has a cost. Accepting trade-offs is not weakness; it is honesty about the limits of time and energy.
Protect the asset

Your health, sleep and mental clarity are the asset that produces everything else. McKeown argues that sleeping well is not a luxury but a strategic choice: an exhausted leader makes poorer decisions on everything that matters.
Design a routine that makes the essential effortless
Instead of relying on willpower every day, build routines in which the important things happen automatically, at the same time and place. Routine frees the mind to focus on what is new and difficult.
faith: O children of Adam, take your adornment at every place of prayer, and eat and drink, but be not excessive. Indeed, He does not like those who commit excess. Moderation, wasatiyyah, runs through Islamic teaching. The Prophet, peace be upon him, also taught that part of a person's good Islam is leaving what does not concern him. Essentialism is that hadith applied to the calendar.
practices: List everything on your plate this month and circle the three that truly matter.
Decline one request this week that scores below 90 percent.
Set a fixed sleep time for the next two weeks and protect it.
reflect: What am I saying yes to that should be a no?
Which problem am I choosing to have?
closing: Choose fewer things, and do them better. Leave what does not concern you, and protect what does.

verses.ar: يَٰبَنِىٓ ءَادَمَ خُذُوا۟ زِينَتَكُمْ عِندَ كُلِّ مَسْجِدٍ وَكُلُوا۟ وَٱشْرَبُوا۟ وَلَا تُسْرِفُوٓا۟ إِنَّهُۥ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُسْرِفِينَ
verses.en: O children of Adam, take your adornment [i.e., wear your clothing] at every masjid, and eat and drink, but be not excessive. Indeed, He likes not those who commit excess.

deep: McKeown argues that the most capable people are often the most overloaded, because their success brings more opportunities than they can handle. Without discipline, success itself becomes the cause of failure, a pattern he calls the paradox of success.

A practical method is to keep a short list of your current essential priorities and check every new request against it. A polite, clear 'no' respects both your time and the other person, who can then find someone better placed to help.

The 90 percent rule forces honest evaluation. Many opportunities seem attractive in the moment but score only 60 or 70 when compared to what truly matters. The rule protects capacity for the rare opportunities that are truly excellent.

Accepting trade-offs openly is liberating. Instead of pretending you can do everything and quietly underperforming, you choose consciously and explain the choice. In leadership, this clarity helps teams focus too.

McKeown notes that many high performers treat sleep as a sacrifice to make. Research suggests sleep deprivation impairs judgement in ways people underestimate. Protecting rest is a strategic choice, and it fits the Qur'anic picture of night as rest and day as work.
Routines remove the need to make the same decisions repeatedly. A fixed time for planning, prayer, reading and exercise turns the essential into the automatic, saving willpower for difficult work.

title: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
author: Stephen R. Covey · 1989
tag: Character first: seven principles that move you from dependence to independence to interdependence.
ideas: Be proactive

Covey's first habit is taking responsibility for your choices. Between what happens to you and how you respond, you have freedom. Proactive people focus on their circle of influence, what they can do, instead of their circle of concern, everything they worry about but cannot control.
Begin with the end in mind

Covey invited readers to imagine their own funeral: what would you want your family, colleagues and community to say about you? That picture becomes a personal mission, and every week's plans should serve it.
Put first things first

He divided tasks into four quadrants by urgency and importance. Effective people live in the second quadrant: important but not urgent, such as planning, relationships, learning and health. Neglect it, and it eventually turns into urgent crises.
Think win-win, and seek first to understand

Effective relationships look for solutions that benefit both sides. And most people listen with the intent to reply rather than to understand. Covey's fifth habit asks you to listen empathically first, then make your case.
Synergise, and sharpen the saw

When people who respect their differences work together, the result can be greater than either could achieve alone. And no one can sustain effectiveness without renewal: physical, mental, social and spiritual. A woodcutter who never stops to sharpen his saw works harder for less.
The emotional bank account

Covey compared trust to a bank account. Keeping promises, kindness, apologies and listening are deposits; broken promises and harshness are withdrawals. With a high balance, small mistakes are forgiven; with an empty one, everything is suspected.
faith: And that there is not for man except that for which he strives, and that his effort is going to be seen, then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense. This is proactivity in the language of revelation: your effort is yours, it is seen, and it will be rewarded. Covey's funeral exercise also echoes the Islamic practice of remembering death to clarify how we should live.
practices: Write a one-paragraph personal mission based on what you would want said at your funeral.
Schedule two 'quadrant two' activities this week before urgent tasks fill the space.
Make one deliberate deposit in an important relationship each day.
reflect: Am I spending my energy in my circle of influence or my circle of concern?
What is the balance in my emotional bank account with my family?
closing: Your effort will be seen. Begin with the end in mind, put first things first, and keep sharpening the saw.

verses.ar: وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَٰنِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَىٰ
verses.en: And that there is not for man except that [good] for which he strives

verses.ar: وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُۥ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ
verses.en: And that his effort is going to be seen -

verses.ar: ثُمَّ يُجْزَىٰهُ ٱلْجَزَآءَ ٱلْأَوْفَىٰ
verses.en: Then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense -

deep: Covey drew on Viktor Frankl's insight that between stimulus and response lies a choice. Proactive people focus energy where they can make a difference, and their circle of influence tends to grow. Reactive people focus on what they cannot control, and their influence shrinks.

Covey suggested writing a personal mission statement covering the roles you hold: servant of Allah, parent, spouse, professional, community member. Reviewing it weekly helps align plans with what matters most.

Quadrant two activities are important but rarely urgent: building relationships, planning, prevention, training others, and personal renewal. Covey recommended weekly planning, scheduling these first before the urgent fills every hour.

Win-win is not weakness; it is the recognition that long-term relationships depend on both sides benefiting. Seeking first to understand means listening until you can state the other person's view to their satisfaction before presenting your own.

Covey described four dimensions of renewal: physical, mental, social-emotional and spiritual. For a believer, the daily prayers, Qur'an, rest and family time are the natural ways to 'sharpen the saw'.

The emotional bank account explains why the same words land differently with different people. Where trust is high, a correction is accepted; where it is low, even a compliment may be suspected. Leaders build balance long before they need to draw on it.

title: The Power of Habit
author: Charles Duhigg · 2012
tag: Understand the loop behind every habit, and you can change it.
ideas: The habit loop

Every habit follows a loop: a cue that triggers the behaviour, a routine, and a reward that tells the brain the loop is worth remembering. Over time the brain stops actively deciding and runs the routine automatically, which is why habits feel so hard to change.
Cravings drive habits

Duhigg explains that habits become powerful when the brain starts anticipating the reward, creating a craving. To build a good habit, make the reward clear and anticipated. To break a bad one, identify what you are really craving: rest, connection, distraction or relief.
The golden rule of habit change

You rarely eliminate a bad habit; you replace it. Keep the same cue and the same reward, but insert a new routine. If stress triggers scrolling for relief, the cue and craving stay, but the routine can become a short walk or dhikr.
Keystone habits

Some habits trigger chain reactions. When Paul O'Neill became chief executive of Alcoa, he focused relentlessly on worker safety. To improve safety, the company had to improve communication and processes, and productivity and profits rose with it. Find the one habit that pulls others along.
Willpower can be trained

Studies Duhigg describes suggest willpower behaves like a muscle that tires with use but grows with practice. Companies like Starbucks trained employees with simple plans for difficult moments, so that self-control became a habit rather than a struggle.
Belief makes change last

Groups such as recovery communities show that habit change sticks best when people believe change is possible, and that belief is often strengthened by being part of a group. We change more easily together than alone.
faith: And by the soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness. He has succeeded who purifies it, and he has failed who corrupts it. The soul has inclinations in both directions; habits shape which way it leans. The Islamic tradition calls this tazkiyah, purification, and it has always worked through repeated practice, good company and replacing harmful routines with remembrance.
practices: Identify the cue, routine and reward of one bad habit.
Keep the cue and reward, but replace the routine with something good for one week.
Pick one keystone habit, such as Fajr on time, and protect it above others.
reflect: What am I really craving when I fall into my worst habit?
Which keystone habit would lift the rest of my life?
closing: Every habit is a loop. Understand it, replace the routine, and purify the soul one repetition at a time.

verses.ar: وَنَفْسٍ وَمَا سَوَّىٰهَا
verses.en: And [by] the soul and He who proportioned it

verses.ar: فَأَلْهَمَهَا فُجُورَهَا وَتَقْوَىٰهَا
verses.en: And inspired it [with discernment of] its wickedness and its righteousness,

verses.ar: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّىٰهَا
verses.en: He has succeeded who purifies it,

verses.ar: وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن دَسَّىٰهَا
verses.en: And he has failed who instills it [with corruption].

deep: Duhigg draws on research at MIT showing that, as a routine becomes automatic, brain activity during the routine drops. This is efficient, but it means habits run without conscious choice. Changing them requires becoming aware of the loop again.

Duhigg describes how marketers learned to create cravings, for example by associating a product with a pleasant sensation. Understanding this helps us notice how our own cravings are being shaped by advertising and apps.

To find the real reward, Duhigg suggests experimenting. If you snack every afternoon, try a walk, a chat or a cup of tea instead, and see which removes the urge. Often the real craving is a break or social contact, not food.

O'Neill's focus on safety required managers to report every injury quickly and propose fixes, which improved communication across the company. A keystone habit in personal life might be praying Fajr on time, which tends to bring earlier sleep, better mornings and more discipline.

Training employees to plan their responses to difficult moments, such as an angry customer, made self-control automatic. The same applies personally: decide in advance how you will respond to known temptations, so that you do not have to rely on willpower in the moment.

Duhigg notes that belief often grows in community. This matches the Islamic emphasis on righteous company and congregational life: we change more easily surrounded by people who expect and support the change.

title: Four Thousand Weeks
author: Oliver Burkeman · 2021
tag: Time management for mortals: the average life is only about four thousand weeks.
ideas: Your life is about four thousand weeks

If you live to around eighty, you get roughly four thousand weeks. Burkeman uses this startling number to shift the question from 'how do I get everything done?' to 'what is worth doing with the little time I have?'
The efficiency trap

The more efficiently you clear tasks, the more tasks arrive. Faster email replies bring more email. Productivity can make you busier without making your life more meaningful. You will never reach the bottom of the list.
Choose what to neglect

Since you cannot do everything, the real skill is deciding what to fail at, consciously. Burkeman suggests limiting work in progress to a few projects at a time, and accepting that many good things will be left undone.
Patience is a power
In a hurried world, the ability to let things take the time they take is a competitive advantage. Real skills, relationships and achievements unfold slowly, and rushing them often ruins them.
The present is the only time you have
Many people treat today as a means to a future that never fully arrives. Burkeman urges finding value in the present activity itself, rather than living perpetually in preparation for later.
Cosmic insignificance is freeing

Seen against the vastness of history, our individual lives are tiny. Burkeman argues this is liberating: you do not need to do something world-changing to have lived a meaningful life. Ordinary acts of care and good work are enough.
faith: He will say: how long did you remain on earth in number of years? They will say: we remained a day or part of a day. He will say: you stayed but a little, if only you had known. On the Day of Judgement, a whole lifetime will feel like a day. Burkeman's four thousand weeks echo this Qur'anic perspective. But Islam adds what his book cannot: ordinary deeds done for Allah are not insignificant at all. They are recorded, multiplied and rewarded.
practices: Calculate roughly how many weeks you have lived, and write the number down.
Limit yourself to three active projects at a time, and park the rest.
Choose one thing to consciously neglect this month without guilt.
reflect: If my life is a day or part of a day, what must it contain?
Where am I living only for a future that may never arrive?
closing: Your weeks are few, but none of them is insignificant to Allah. Choose wisely, act today, and let the rest go.

verses.ar: قَٰلَ كَمْ لَبِثْتُمْ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ عَدَدَ سِنِينَ
verses.en: [Allāh] will say, "How long did you remain on earth in number of years?"

verses.ar: قَالُوا۟ لَبِثْنَا يَوْمًا أَوْ بَعْضَ يَوْمٍ فَسْـَٔلِ ٱلْعَآدِّينَ
verses.en: They will say, "We remained a day or part of a day; ask those who enumerate."

verses.ar: قَٰلَ إِن لَّبِثْتُمْ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا لَّوْ أَنَّكُمْ كُنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ
verses.en: He will say, "You stayed not but a little - if only you had known.

deep: The number is striking because it is small. Burkeman uses it not to cause anxiety but to encourage clarity. When time is seen as finite, the question shifts from optimising to choosing, and from accumulating experiences to committing deeply to a few.

Burkeman observes that the more efficient people become, the more work flows to them. He calls this the efficiency trap. The solution is not to work faster but to decide in advance what matters and accept that much will remain undone.
He suggests keeping a short list of no more than three to ten active tasks, and adding a new one only when one is finished. This forces prioritisation and makes progress visible.

Patience, in Burkeman's sense, means accepting that important things take time and resisting the urge to rush or quit. It aligns with the Qur'anic praise of sabr and the prophetic warning that haste is from Shaytan.

Burkeman warns against treating today as a stepping stone to a future where life will finally begin. The present moment is where life happens; neglecting it in pursuit of a later fulfilment means missing life itself.

Burkeman's framing is secular, and Islam adds a vital correction. Individual lives are small on a cosmic scale, but in the sight of Allah, sincere deeds are recorded and rewarded, however small. The believer can enjoy ordinary good without anxiety about grand legacy.

title: The Book of Character
author: Ibn Hazm of Córdoba · 11th century
tag: An Andalusian scholar's honest notes on driving away worry, friendship and curing the soul.
ideas: Every human being is fleeing the same thing

Ibn Hazm observed that all people, whatever their religion, wealth or rank, share one goal: to drive away worry. The merchant chases profit, the scholar chases knowledge, the pleasure-seeker chases pleasure, all to escape anxiety. He then concluded that only one pursuit removes worry completely, because only one goal cannot be taken from you: working for Allah and the Hereafter.
Test your path by what it frees you from

Every worldly goal, he noted, brings new worries with it: wealth brings fear of loss, fame brings fear of falling, love brings fear of separation. Ask of any ambition: when I reach it, will I be calmer, or will I have something new to guard? A path worth giving your life to is one whose end does not need guarding.
Knowledge is its own reward

Ibn Hazm wrote that if knowledge brought no other benefit than to make the ignorant respect you and the learned love you, that alone would be enough reason to seek it. But its real gift is inner: it frees the mind from confusion and the heart from many anxieties that come from not understanding the world.
Praise and blame should not own you
