He warned that a person whose peace depends on what others say has handed his heart to strangers. The wise person, he taught, examines whether praise or criticism is true. If true, act on it; if false, let it pass. Either way, your character is your own work, not the crowd's.
Look honestly at your own faults

Unusually for his time, Ibn Hazm described defects in his own character and how he struggled to cure them, treating the soul as a patient and himself as its physician. He urged readers to do the same: name your faults plainly, then work on them steadily, without despair and without pretending.
Friendship is tested, not declared

He gave careful advice on friendship: choose friends for their religion and character, not for benefit; correct a friend privately and gently, since advice given in public becomes rebuke; and do not abandon a friend over one mistake. True friends, he noted, are rare, so guard the ones you find.
faith: He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself, remembers the name of his Lord and prays. But you prefer the worldly life, while the Hereafter is better and more enduring. These verses confirm Ibn Hazm's discovery: the worldly life is preferred, but it cannot give the lasting relief the soul seeks. Purification of the self and remembrance of Allah are the only goals whose reward is both better and more enduring.
practices: Write down your top three worries, and ask which goal each one is attached to.
Name one fault of your own honestly, and choose one small step to treat it this week.
Correct someone you care about only in private, and gently.
reflect: Which of my goals brings more worry the closer I get to it?
Whose praise or blame has too much power over my heart?
closing: Everyone is running from worry. Ibn Hazm points to the only road that truly leads away from it: purify the soul, and work for what endures.

verses.ar: قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن تَزَكَّىٰ
verses.en: He has certainly succeeded who purifies himself

verses.ar: وَذَكَرَ ٱسْمَ رَبِّهِۦ فَصَلَّىٰ
verses.en: And mentions the name of his Lord and prays.

verses.ar: بَلْ تُؤْثِرُونَ ٱلْحَيَوٰةَ ٱلدُّنْيَا
verses.en: But you prefer the worldly life,

verses.ar: وَٱلْـَٔاخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰٓ
verses.en: While the Hereafter is better and more enduring.

deep: Ibn Hazm reached this conclusion after observing people across his life at court and in exile. His point is not that worldly goals are wrong, but that none of them can fully deliver what people want from them. A promotion relieves one worry and creates another: keeping it. Only a goal that death cannot take away removes worry at its root.

In practice, before accepting a new role, title or investment, list the new worries it will bring alongside the benefits. A wise person still accepts many such goals, but with open eyes, holding them lightly and anchoring the heart in what lasts.

For a professional, this means valuing learning for its own sake, not only for certificates or promotions. The scholar who reads to understand gains a calm that the one reading only to impress never finds, because understanding cannot be taken away by a change of employer.

Ibn Hazm suggests a simple test: when someone praises you, ask whether it is true; if it is, thank Allah, and if not, do not be deceived. When someone criticises you, ask the same question; if it is true, correct yourself, and if not, it cannot harm you. Your worth is decided by your conduct and by Allah, not by the crowd.

Treating the soul like a patient means being specific. 'I am impatient' is too vague to cure. 'I interrupt colleagues when I already know the answer' can be worked on. Ibn Hazm's honesty about himself is an invitation to name our own faults precisely, and to treat them steadily over months, not with one burst of resolution.

In professional life this applies to colleagues and partners too. Choose those you trust closely for their integrity, not their usefulness. Correct them privately. And when a trusted friend fails once, remember the many years of good before deciding the relationship is over.

title: Letter to a Disciple
author: Imam al-Ghazali · Ayyuha al-Walad
tag: A student asked his teacher for advice. The answer is still one of the most direct letters in Islamic literature.
ideas: Knowledge without action is wasted

A former student wrote to al-Ghazali saying he had spent years studying and wanted to know which knowledge would truly benefit him. Al-Ghazali answered bluntly: knowledge without action is madness, and action without knowledge does not happen. Learning that never changes your conduct is a burden, not a treasure.
Advice is easy; accepting it is hard

Al-Ghazali told his student that giving advice is simple, but accepting it is difficult, because it tastes bitter to those who follow their desires. The test of a seeker is not how much advice he collects, but how much he swallows and lives by.
Four things to leave

He listed four things to avoid. Do not get into arguments for the sake of winning, because debate hardens hearts. Do not become a preacher to others before you practise what you preach. Do not mix with rulers in ways that corrupt your religion. And do not accept their gifts, which create obligations you cannot carry.
Four things to do

Then four things to do. Treat Allah the way you would want a servant to treat you. Treat people the way you would want to be treated. Seek only the knowledge that reforms your heart and prepares you for death. And do not store up more provision than you need for a year, trusting Allah for the rest.
Your time is your capital

Al-Ghazali reminded his student that every breath is a jewel that cannot be replaced. He warned against spending nights in study that brings status but not closeness to Allah. Ask of each hour: if this were my last, would I be glad to meet my Lord with it?
The night prayer is the student's secret

He urged his student to rise before dawn and seek forgiveness, quoting the advice attributed to Luqman to his son: do not let the rooster be wiser than you, calling out before dawn while you sleep. The prayer of the night, he said, polishes the heart in a way daytime learning cannot.
faith: O you who believe, why do you say what you do not do? Great is hatred in the sight of Allah that you say what you do not do. Al-Ghazali's whole letter is a commentary on these verses. Ibn Kathir notes that they were revealed about people who spoke of deeds they then failed to do. Knowledge brings accountability: the more we know, the more we will be asked about what we did with it.
practices: Take one thing you already know you should do, and do it this week before learning anything new.
Avoid one argument you would normally enter just to win.
Pray two rak'ahs before Fajr at least twice this week.
reflect: How much of what I know am I actually living?
Which of al-Ghazali's four warnings speaks most to my life now?
closing: Knowledge is a trust, not a trophy. Learn what reforms your heart, and act on what you learn.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ لِمَ تَقُولُونَ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ
verses.en: O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?

verses.ar: كَبُرَ مَقْتًا عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَن تَقُولُوا۟ مَا لَا تَفْعَلُونَ
verses.en: Greatly hateful in the sight of Allāh is that you say what you do not do.

deep: Al-Ghazali was speaking from experience. He had been the most celebrated professor in Baghdad, yet he left his post because he felt his knowledge had not changed his heart. His advice to the student is the lesson he learned at great personal cost: learning that does not shape conduct is incomplete.

Ask yourself which piece of advice you have heard many times but never acted on. That is usually the one that matters most. The bitterness al-Ghazali describes is a sign that the advice is touching something real.

These warnings were written for scholars, but their spirit applies to any professional. Avoid arguing to win rather than to find the truth. Practise before you advise. Be careful with relationships with the powerful that compromise your independence, and with gifts that create silent obligations, a principle every compliance officer will recognise.

The year's provision point is not a rule against saving or investment; scholars have always permitted prudent planning. It is a warning against hoarding out of fear. The four positive points together form a complete ethic: integrity with Allah, fairness with people, purposeful learning, and trust.

Al-Ghazali's image of breaths as jewels is a call to audit how time is spent. A useful practice is to look back at the last week and mark which hours brought you closer to Allah, to your family, or to useful work, and which were simply lost.

He believed the night prayer has a unique effect on the heart because it is done when no one sees, when the world is quiet and the soul is honest. Even two short rak'ahs before Fajr can, over months, change the quality of a person's day.

title: Al-Fawa'id: Pearls of Benefit
author: Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah · 14th century
tag: Short reflections from one of Islam's great physicians of the heart.
ideas: Ten things that bring no benefit

Ibn al-Qayyim listed ten things that are of no use: knowledge not acted upon, action without sincerity, wealth not spent in good, a heart empty of love for Allah, a body not used in obedience, love that does not seek Allah's pleasure, time not used to make up for what was missed, thought spent on what does not matter, serving someone who does not bring you closer to Allah, and fear and hope placed in a creature who holds neither.
Wasted time is worse than death

He wrote that wasting time is worse than death, because death cuts you off from this world, while wasting time cuts you off from Allah and the Hereafter. Every hour has a price, whether we pay attention to it or not.
How a sin is born

He traced the path of wrongdoing: it begins as a passing thought, the thought becomes an idea, the idea becomes a desire, the desire becomes a resolve, and the resolve becomes an action that hardens into habit. The easiest place to stop is the first step: push away the thought before it grows roots.
The world is like a shadow

A well-known image from his writing compares the world to a shadow: chase it, and it runs ahead of you; turn your back on it and walk towards the light, and it follows you. Those who make the Hereafter their goal often find the world comes to them anyway.
Leadership in religion comes from two things

Commenting on the verse about leaders who guide by Allah's command, Ibn al-Qayyim, following his teacher Ibn Taymiyyah, explained that leadership in religion is reached through patience and certainty. Patience restrains the self from desire; certainty removes doubt. Together they produce people worth following.
The heart has its own illnesses

He wrote that the heart can fall ill and even die, just like the body, and that sins are its poisons while remembrance of Allah is its food. A person who feels no pain at his own sins should worry, because a dead heart feels nothing.
faith: And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and had certainty in Our signs. Patience and certainty are the two wings Ibn al-Qayyim returns to throughout al-Fawa'id. Patience is the discipline of the self; certainty is the clarity of faith. Leadership, in work and in religion, rests on both.
practices: Check yourself against the list of ten useless things, and pick one to remove.
When a harmful thought arrives, replace it immediately with dhikr.
Spend five quiet minutes daily on muhasabah, taking account of your heart.
reflect: Which of the ten useless things is most present in my life?
Is my heart still pained by my mistakes?
closing: Ibn al-Qayyim's pearls are short, but each one is a mirror. Look into them honestly, and heal the heart while it is still alive.

verses.ar: وَجَعَلْنَا مِنْهُمْ أَئِمَّةً يَهْدُونَ بِأَمْرِنَا لَمَّا صَبَرُوا۟ وَكَانُوا۟ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا يُوقِنُونَ
verses.en: And We made from among them leaders guiding by Our command when they were patient and [when] they were certain of Our signs.

deep: Each item on this list describes something that looks valuable but has been emptied of its benefit. Knowledge without action, wealth without spending, a body without obedience. The list is useful as a monthly self-audit: which of the ten describes something I am holding right now?

Ibn al-Qayyim's comparison is deliberately shocking. Death is certain and outside our control; wasted time is a choice. We grieve the first and barely notice the second. The scholars of the early generations were known to guard their time more carefully than their money.

This chain explains why habits are so hard to break once established. It also gives hope: there are several places to interrupt the chain. Guard what you look at and listen to, replace harmful thoughts with remembrance, and seek company that pulls you towards good before the resolve forms.

The image does not mean we should neglect our work or responsibilities. It means our intentions should be directed towards Allah and the Hereafter, and the world is then pursued as a means, not as the goal. Many people who chase only status find it always just out of reach.

Patience restrains the self from following desires and from panic in hardship. Certainty clears away doubts about Allah's promise. A leader with patience but no certainty becomes stubborn; one with certainty but no patience becomes reckless. Together they produce trustworthy leadership.

Ibn al-Qayyim lists signs of a sick heart: it no longer feels pain at its sins, finds no sweetness in worship, and is more attached to creation than to the Creator. The cure begins with recognising the illness, then with remembrance, the Qur'an, repentance and good company.

title: The Book of Wisdoms
author: Ibn Ata'illah al-Iskandari · al-Hikam
tag: Aphorisms that have guided seekers for seven centuries, each one a lesson in trust.
ideas: Rely on Allah, not on your deeds

The first aphorism of the Hikam says that a sign of relying on your own deeds is losing hope when you slip. Good deeds matter, but if your hope rests on them rather than on Allah's mercy, every failure will crush you. Rely on the Giver, and failure becomes a reason to return, not to despair.
Striving for the guaranteed

Ibn Ata'illah warned that striving for what is already guaranteed to you, your provision, while neglecting what is required of you, your obedience, is a sign of clouded insight. We often worry about the one thing Allah has promised, and relax about the one thing He has asked.
Do not wait for free time

He called it foolishness of the soul to postpone good deeds until you have more free time. Free time rarely comes, and when it does, other distractions fill it. The deed you delay today is usually the deed you never do.
Sometimes He gives by withholding

One of his most quoted lines teaches that sometimes Allah gives to you by depriving you, and deprives you by giving to you. A closed door may protect you; an open one may test you. Judge your circumstances by what they do to your heart, not by how comfortable they feel.
Bury your existence

He taught that a seed buried in the ground grows strong roots, while one left on the surface withers. In the same way, sincerity grows in obscurity. Doing good unseen, without need for recognition, builds the roots that allow a person to bear fruit later.
Few deeds, but He opened the door

When Allah opens a door for you to know Him, Ibn Ata'illah wrote, do not worry that your deeds are few. He did not open it because of your deeds; He opened it because He wanted to make Himself known to you. Walk through it with gratitude.
faith: And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I respond to the call of the caller when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me, that they may be rightly guided. The whole of the Hikam flows from this nearness. Allah is closer than our anxieties suggest, and the path to Him begins with turning, not with perfect deeds.
practices: After a mistake this week, make du'a immediately instead of dwelling on guilt.
Do one good deed today that you have been postponing for 'when I have time'.
Reflect on one closed door in your life and ask what it may have protected you from.
reflect: Is my hope in Allah, or in my own record?
Which good deed am I waiting for 'free time' to do?
closing: He is near, and He responds. Rely on His mercy, act today, and trust His giving even when it looks like withholding.

verses.ar: وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِى عَنِّى فَإِنِّى قَرِيبٌ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ ٱلدَّاعِ إِذَا دَعَانِ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا۟ لِى وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا۟ بِى لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ
verses.en: And when My servants ask you, [O Muḥammad], concerning Me - indeed I am near. I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me [by obedience] and believe in Me that they may be [rightly] guided.

deep: This aphorism protects against two extremes. Some people do good deeds and become proud; others slip and despair. Both are relying on their own record. The believer works hard, but places hope in Allah's mercy, so that success brings gratitude and failure brings repentance rather than despair.

Provision is decreed and will reach you; obedience is what you will be asked about. Yet our worries usually run the other way. This does not mean we stop working, because taking the means is itself obedience. It means our anxiety should be about our character and worship, not about whether Allah will provide.

The commentators explain that postponing deeds until one is 'free' assumes we will have time later, which no one is promised. Small deeds done now, a short prayer, a kind word, a little charity, are better than great deeds planned for a tomorrow that may not come.

Many people can look back at a rejection, a failed plan or a loss that later proved to be a protection or the start of something better. Ibn Ata'illah asks us to trust this wisdom while the outcome is still hidden, not only after we understand it.

This applies to professional reputation as well as spirituality. People who build quietly, mastering their craft and serving without seeking credit, often become the most trusted. Seeking visibility too early can produce a shallow root that cannot support later responsibility.

This aphorism is an antidote to discouragement. Many people feel unworthy of closeness to Allah because their deeds are few. Ibn Ata'illah reminds them that Allah's invitation precedes our worthiness. The right response is not hesitation but gratitude and walking forward.

title: The Forty Hadith
author: Imam al-Nawawi · 13th century
tag: A compact collection of prophetic sayings that scholars say contains the foundations of the religion.
hadith: Actions are only by intentions, and every person will have only what he intended.
Sahih al-Bukhari 1, Sahih Muslim 1907
ideas: It begins with intention

Imam al-Nawawi opened his collection, as al-Bukhari did, with the hadith that actions are judged by intentions. The scholars placed it first because every deed of worship, work or family life is shaped by why it is done. The same act can be worship or vanity depending on the heart behind it.
Leave what does not concern you

The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that part of the excellence of a person's Islam is leaving what does not concern him, as recorded by al-Tirmidhi. In an age of endless news, gossip and opinions, this single sentence protects time, attention and the heart.
Do not become angry

A man asked the Prophet for advice, and he said: do not become angry. The man repeated his request several times, and each time the answer was the same, as recorded by al-Bukhari. The scholars explain that anger opens the door to most harms, so closing it protects a great deal.
Love for your brother what you love for yourself

None of you truly believes, the Prophet said, until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself, in a hadith in both Sahihs. This turns ethics into a simple test: would I want this done to me? It applies in trade, in management, and at home.
Three instructions for every day

The Prophet told Abu Dharr and Mu'adh: fear Allah wherever you are, follow a bad deed with a good one that will erase it, and treat people with good character, as recorded by al-Tirmidhi. Taqwa, repair and manners: a complete daily programme in one sentence.
Be in this world like a stranger

Taking Ibn 'Umar by the shoulder, the Prophet said: be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveller, in a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari. A traveller uses what he needs, does not become attached to the road, and keeps his eyes on his destination.
faith: There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example for anyone whose hope is in Allah and the Last Day and who remembers Allah often. Al-Nawawi gathered these hadith so that the example of the Prophet, peace be upon him, could be carried in memory and practised in daily life. Each hadith is short enough to memorise and deep enough to study for a lifetime.
practices: Memorise one of these hadith this week, and repeat it before work each morning.
Leave one source of news or gossip that does not concern you.
When anger rises, remember the three-word advice: do not become angry.
reflect: Which of these hadith would change my week most if I truly lived it?
Where am I spending attention on what does not concern me?
closing: Forty sayings, carried in the heart, can shape a whole life. Begin with intention, and walk like a traveller.

verses.ar: لَّقَدْ كَانَ لَكُمْ فِى رَسُولِ ٱللَّهِ أُسْوَةٌ حَسَنَةٌ لِّمَن كَانَ يَرْجُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَٱلْيَوْمَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَ وَذَكَرَ ٱللَّهَ كَثِيرًا
verses.en: There has certainly been for you in the Messenger of Allāh an excellent pattern for anyone whose hope is in Allāh and the Last Day and [who] remembers Allāh often.

deep: The scholars said this hadith applies to everything a Muslim does, which is why it is placed first. Practically, it encourages a brief pause before work, family duties and even rest, renewing the intention so that ordinary actions become acts of worship.

Al-Nawawi's commentators explain that 'what does not concern you' includes unnecessary curiosity, idle talk and involvement in affairs that are not your responsibility. Applied today, it is a powerful filter for social media, workplace gossip and endless news.

Ibn Rajab explains that the advice covers two things: avoiding the causes of anger, and not acting on anger when it comes. The Sunnah gives practical remedies: seeking refuge in Allah, changing posture, staying silent and making ablution.

This standard is demanding because it applies even when we have power over others. In business, it means pricing, contracts and treatment of staff that we would accept if we were on the other side. Scholars note it includes wanting guidance and goodness for others, not only material benefit.

Taqwa wherever you are means the same conduct in private and in public. Following a bad deed with a good one recognises that we will slip, and gives a way to repair. Good character with people completes it, because faith that harms people is incomplete.

Ibn 'Umar, who narrated this hadith, used to add: when you reach the evening, do not wait for the morning, and when you reach the morning, do not wait for the evening. The traveller's mindset is not neglect of the world; it is freedom from attachment to it.

title: The Muqaddimah
author: Ibn Khaldun · 1377
tag: The North African scholar who explained why nations rise and fall, centuries before modern social science.
ideas: Group solidarity builds states

Ibn Khaldun's central concept is 'asabiyyah: the group feeling, loyalty and cohesion that bind people together. Groups with strong 'asabiyyah, often hardened by difficult desert or rural life, are able to conquer and build. As they settle into comfort and luxury, that cohesion weakens.
Dynasties follow a life cycle

He observed that ruling families tend to last about three or four generations. The founders build with sacrifice; the next generation maintains what they saw built; the third imitates without understanding; and the fourth, born into luxury, loses what it never had to earn. The pattern still describes many family businesses.
Injustice ruins civilisation

One of the chapters of the Muqaddimah states plainly that injustice brings about the ruin of civilisation. When rulers seize property, overtax or oppress, people lose the incentive to work and build, and prosperity collapses. For Ibn Khaldun, justice was not only a moral duty but an economic necessity.
Lower taxes can raise more revenue

He noticed that at the start of a dynasty, taxes are low and revenue is high, because people are encouraged to work and trade. Later, rulers raise taxes to pay for luxury, activity falls, and revenue shrinks. Modern economists have acknowledged him as an early thinker on this idea.
Humans are social by nature

Ibn Khaldun argued that no individual can meet all his needs alone; cooperation and the division of labour are what make civilisation possible. Cities grow because people specialise and exchange, which is why the quality of trust and law in a society determines its wealth.
The defeated imitate the victor

He observed that conquered peoples tend to imitate their conquerors in dress, customs and ideas, believing their success comes from those habits. It is a sharp insight into cultural confidence, and a warning to societies that copy the surface of others' success without its substance.
faith: And your Lord would not have destroyed the cities unjustly while their people were reformers. Ibn Khaldun's analysis rests on this Qur'anic law: societies are sustained by reform and justice, and ruined by corruption and oppression. His genius was to show how this moral truth works through economics, politics and human psychology.
practices: Identify which 'generation' your organisation or family business is in, and what it needs to avoid decline.
Look for one place in your work where unfairness is quietly reducing people's motivation.
Read one short extract from the Muqaddimah in translation this month.
reflect: Am I building with sacrifice, or living off what others built?
Where is justice the hidden foundation of the results I want?
closing: Nations rise on cohesion and justice, and fall when comfort breeds complacency. Ibn Khaldun's map is six centuries old, and still accurate.

verses.ar: وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ لِيُهْلِكَ ٱلْقُرَىٰ بِظُلْمٍ وَأَهْلُهَا مُصْلِحُونَ
verses.en: And your Lord would not have destroyed the cities unjustly while their people were reformers.

deep: 'Asabiyyah is not only tribal loyalty; it is any strong sense of shared purpose and mutual commitment. Startups, reform movements and new institutions often have it in abundance. Ibn Khaldun's warning is that success and comfort tend to dissolve the very cohesion that produced success.

Ibn Khaldun's generational model is a pattern, not a law. Many family firms in Nigeria face the second and third generation challenge. The antidote he implies is deliberately passing on not only wealth but the founder's discipline, values and sense of mission.

Ibn Khaldun argued that when people's property and earnings are not secure, they stop working and investing, and the whole economy declines. This makes justice, contract enforcement and protection from arbitrary seizure the foundation of prosperity, not merely moral ideals.

His observation was that high rates eventually reduce revenue because activity falls. The broader lesson concerns incentives: policies that take too much from productive people discourage the production they depend on.

Because cooperation creates wealth, the quality of trust and institutions in a society shapes its prosperity. Where contracts are honoured and people can rely on each other, specialisation and trade grow; where trust is low, everyone must do everything themselves.

This insight speaks to post-colonial societies, including Nigeria. Imitating the outward forms of successful nations, their dress, slogans or institutional names, does not reproduce their success. What matters is the substance: discipline, justice, learning and cohesion.

title: Mindset
author: Carol S. Dweck · 2006
tag: Whether you believe ability is fixed or can grow shapes almost everything you do.
ideas: Two mindsets

Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck found that people hold one of two beliefs about ability. In a fixed mindset, intelligence and talent are fixed traits, so every challenge is a test of worth. In a growth mindset, abilities can be developed through effort, strategy and help, so challenges are opportunities to grow.
Failure means different things

For someone with a fixed mindset, failure is a verdict: I am not good enough. For someone with a growth mindset, failure is information: this strategy did not work yet. The same event produces shame in one person and learning in another.
Praise the process, not the person

Dweck's studies with children showed that praising intelligence made them avoid harder tasks to protect their image, while praising effort and strategy made them seek challenges. How we praise our children and staff shapes how they handle difficulty.
The power of 'not yet'

Some schools replaced failing grades with 'not yet', signalling that the student is on a learning curve. The phrase turns a closed door into a path. It works in offices and families as well as classrooms.
Leaders and the fixed mindset

Dweck describes leaders who surround themselves with admirers, punish bad news and need to be the smartest in the room. Their fixed mindset makes them brittle. Growth-minded leaders hire people better than themselves and treat mistakes as learning.
False growth mindset

Dweck later warned that growth mindset is not just praising effort or being positive. Effort that uses the same failing strategy is not growth. Real growth mindset combines effort with new strategies and seeking input from others.
faith: Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man that which he knew not. The first revelation was a command to learn, and a reminder that knowledge is a gift from Allah. The believer's mindset is one of growth by nature: always a student, always asking 'My Lord, increase me in knowledge'.
practices: Replace 'I'm not good at this' with 'I'm not good at this yet' for one week.
When praising your children or team, name the effort and strategy, not the talent.
Ask someone for a new strategy on a problem you keep failing at.
reflect: In which area of my life do I hold a fixed mindset?
How do I react when someone outperforms me?
closing: Ability grows. Read, learn, try new strategies, and remember that the first word of revelation was a command to learn.

verses.ar: ٱقْرَأْ بِٱسْمِ رَبِّكَ ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَ
verses.en: Recite in the name of your Lord who created –

verses.ar: خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ
verses.en: Created man from a clinging substance.

verses.ar: ٱقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ ٱلْأَكْرَمُ
verses.en: Recite, and your Lord is the most Generous -

verses.ar: ٱلَّذِى عَلَّمَ بِٱلْقَلَمِ
verses.en: Who taught by the pen –

verses.ar: عَلَّمَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مَا لَمْ يَعْلَمْ
verses.en: Taught man that which he knew not.

deep: Dweck's research began with children solving puzzles that became too hard. Some became discouraged; others became excited, saying they loved a challenge. That difference in belief about ability shaped their persistence and performance.

Dweck notes that people can hold a fixed mindset in one area and a growth mindset in another. The goal is to notice the fixed-mindset voice, the one that says 'maybe you are not good at this', and answer it with a growth-oriented response.

In one well-known study, children praised for intelligence later chose easier tasks and performed worse after failure, while those praised for effort chose harder tasks and improved. Praise teaches children what we value.
'Not yet' changes how both students and adults see a gap. Instead of a final verdict, it frames current ability as a point on a path, which encourages continued effort and learning.

Dweck describes 'CEO disease': leaders who need constant validation, surround themselves with admirers and punish dissent. Their organisations stop learning. Growth-minded leaders build cultures where people can grow and admit mistakes.

Dweck clarified that a growth mindset is not just effort or optimism. It means believing ability can grow and acting on that belief by trying new strategies, seeking feedback and learning from setbacks.

title: Man's Search for Meaning
author: Viktor E. Frankl · 1946
tag: A psychiatrist who survived the Nazi camps found that meaning is the deepest human need.
ideas: Meaning helped people survive

Viktor Frankl, a Viennese psychiatrist, was imprisoned in Nazi concentration camps, including Auschwitz. He observed that prisoners who held on to a purpose, a loved one to return to or a task to complete, were more likely to endure. Those who lost all sense of meaning often gave up.
The last human freedom

Frankl wrote that everything can be taken from a person except one thing: the freedom to choose one's attitude in any set of circumstances. Even in the camps, some prisoners gave away their last piece of bread. Circumstances limit us, but they do not decide who we are.
Three sources of meaning

Frankl founded logotherapy, a therapy centred on meaning. He described three paths to it: creating a work or doing a deed; experiencing something or loving someone; and the attitude we take towards unavoidable suffering.
Meaning is found, not invented

Frankl argued that we do not simply invent meaning; we discover it in the demands of each situation. Instead of asking what we expect from life, we should ask what life expects from us, and answer through responsible action.
Happiness cannot be pursued directly
Frankl observed that happiness and success, when aimed at directly, tend to escape us. They come as side effects of dedication to a cause greater than oneself or love for another person.
A 'why' makes almost any 'how' bearable
Frankl often quoted Nietzsche's line that one who has a why to live can bear almost any how. People can endure astonishing hardship when they know what it is for.
faith: And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me. The Qur'an answers the question Frankl spent his life on: the ultimate why. Worship, 'ibadah, in its full Islamic sense, includes every good act done for Allah: work, love, patience and service. Frankl's three sources of meaning all find their home in this one purpose.
practices: Write one sentence that answers: what does my life expect of me right now?
Reframe one current hardship by asking what attitude Allah would love from me in it.
Do one act of service this week purely for the sake of Allah.
reflect: What is my 'why' on the hardest days?
Am I chasing happiness directly, or serving something greater?
closing: Everything can be taken except your response. Know your why, and let it be the one Allah created you for.

verses.ar: وَمَا خَلَقْتُ ٱلْجِنَّ وَٱلْإِنسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ
verses.en: And I did not create the jinn and mankind except to worship Me.

deep: Frankl noticed that the prisoners who lost all sense of purpose often stopped fighting for survival. Meaning, whether a person, a task or a faith, gave others the strength to endure extraordinary suffering.

This freedom is not about denying pain. It is about choosing how we respond to it. Frankl saw prisoners give away their last bread and comfort others, showing that dignity can survive even when everything external is gone.

In logotherapy, a person in despair is helped to discover meaning through what they can give, what they can receive and love, and how they choose to bear what cannot be changed. All three remain available in almost any situation.

Frankl's reversal of the question, from what I expect from life to what life expects from me, shifts focus from entitlement to responsibility. In Islamic terms, it echoes the awareness that every situation is a test and an opportunity to respond well.

Frankl argued that happiness ensues; it cannot be pursued. Aiming directly at it tends to make it slip away. It comes as a by-product of living for something greater, which Islam identifies as living for Allah.

This idea explains why people with a strong sense of purpose cope better with hardship. For a believer, the ultimate why gives meaning to every how: patience, effort and even suffering become acts of worship.

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius · 2nd century
tag: The private notebook of a Roman emperor training himself to be good.
ideas: A journal never meant for readers

Marcus Aurelius was the most powerful man in the Roman world, yet his Meditations were private notes reminding himself how to live: with self-discipline, justice and humility. Their honesty is why they still speak to leaders today.
Prepare for difficult people

He began some mornings by reminding himself that he would meet people who were ungrateful, arrogant or dishonest, and that they acted from ignorance. Expecting it in advance helped him respond with patience instead of anger.
Focus on what is in your control

Following the Stoic teacher Epictetus, Marcus separated what is up to us, our judgements, intentions and actions, from what is not, other people, reputation and events. Peace comes from investing energy in the first and accepting the second.
The obstacle becomes the way

He wrote that what stands in the way of action can itself become the path of action. A difficult colleague becomes a lesson in patience; a setback becomes training in resilience. Nothing is wasted if you use it.
Remember death

Marcus repeatedly reminded himself that life is short, that emperors before him were forgotten, and that he too would die. This was not gloom; it was clarity. Remembering death made it easier to act rightly today.
Do the next right thing
Rather than dreaming of grand achievements, he urged himself to do the task in front of him as if it were the last act of his life, with care, without pretence, and without complaint.
faith: No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a register before We bring it into being. That is easy for Allah, in order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult over what He has given you. Islam gives the Stoic's calm a deeper foundation: events are not blind fate but Allah's decree, written with wisdom. Remembering death, which the Prophet, peace be upon him, called the destroyer of pleasures, is likewise part of the believer's daily clarity.
practices: Each morning, prepare yourself for one difficult interaction and decide your response in advance.
Write two columns: what is in my control today, and what is not.
End the day by asking: did I act today as if it were my last?
reflect: Which obstacle in front of me could become my path?
How would I live this week if I remembered death more often?
closing: Expect difficulty, control what is yours, accept the decree, and do the next right thing well.

verses.ar: مَآ أَصَابَ مِن مُّصِيبَةٍ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ وَلَا فِىٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ إِلَّا فِى كِتَٰبٍ مِّن قَبْلِ أَن نَّبْرَأَهَآ إِنَّ ذَٰلِكَ عَلَى ٱللَّهِ يَسِيرٌ
verses.en: No disaster strikes upon the earth or among yourselves except that it is in a register before We bring it into being - indeed that, for Allāh, is easy -

verses.ar: لِّكَيْلَا تَأْسَوْا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَاتَكُمْ وَلَا تَفْرَحُوا۟ بِمَآ ءَاتَىٰكُمْ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ كُلَّ مُخْتَالٍ فَخُورٍ
verses.en: In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you. And Allāh does not like everyone self-deluded and boastful -

deep: Marcus wrote his notes during wars and plagues, often in camp at night. That context makes them powerful: they are not abstract theory but a busy leader's attempts to keep his character steady under pressure.
Marcus reminded himself that people who behave badly do so from ignorance of what is good, and that he shared their nature. Preparing in advance helped him respond with patience instead of anger.
This distinction, taught by Epictetus, frees attention for what matters. For a professional, it means focusing on preparation, honesty and effort, and accepting the outcome with calm.
Marcus wrote that the impediment to action advances action. A difficult situation becomes an opportunity to practise patience, wisdom or courage. Nothing that happens is wasted if it is used to grow.

Marcus often contemplated mortality to keep perspective. The Prophet, peace be upon him, also advised remembering death frequently, calling it the destroyer of pleasures, as a way to keep life in proper perspective.

He urged himself to do each task as if it were the last of his life: carefully, sincerely and without complaint. This is close to the Islamic concept of ihsan, doing things with excellence because Allah sees you.

title: Grit
author: Angela Duckworth · 2016
tag: Passion and perseverance for long-term goals predict success more than talent.
ideas: Talent is not enough

Psychologist Angela Duckworth studied cadets at West Point, spelling competitors and salespeople, and found that a combination of passion and perseverance, which she called grit, often predicted success better than talent or intelligence.
Effort counts twice

Her formula: talent multiplied by effort equals skill, and skill multiplied by effort equals achievement. Effort appears twice. A less talented person who keeps working can overtake a more talented one who stops.
A hierarchy of goals

Gritty people have a top-level goal that gives direction to everything else, with many lower-level goals beneath it. If one lower goal fails, they find another route, but they do not abandon the top one.
Deliberate practice

Grit is not just working long hours. Duckworth draws on research showing experts improve through deliberate practice: focused work on specific weaknesses, with clear goals and immediate feedback, which is often uncomfortable.
Purpose deepens passion
Over time, the grittiest people connect their work to a purpose beyond themselves, to helping others. Interest starts the journey; purpose sustains it through decades.
The hard thing rule

In her family, everyone must do one hard thing that requires daily practice, may quit only at a natural endpoint such as the end of a season, and chooses the hard thing themselves. It is a simple way to grow grit in children.
faith: O you who believe, persevere, and endure, and remain stationed, and fear Allah that you may be successful. The verse uses three related words: sabr, patience; musabarah, outlasting in patience; and murabatah, remaining firmly at your post. Ibn Kathir explains it as steadfastness in obedience and in facing difficulty. Grit, in the Qur'anic sense, is patience that lasts and does not leave its post.
practices: Write your top-level goal, and three lower-level goals that serve it.
Spend 20 minutes this week on deliberate practice of one specific weakness.
Introduce the hard thing rule to your children in a simple form.
reflect: Where do I quit too early?
How does my daily work connect to a purpose beyond me?
closing: Effort counts twice. Persevere, outlast, and stay at your post.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱصْبِرُوا۟ وَصَابِرُوا۟ وَرَابِطُوا۟ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ
verses.en: O you who have believed, persevere and endure and remain stationed and fear Allāh that you may be successful.

deep: Duckworth studied West Point cadets during their gruelling first summer. The ones who stayed were not necessarily the most talented, but scored higher on her grit scale, measuring passion and perseverance for long-term goals.

Her formula captures why effort matters so much: effort builds skill, and effort applied to skill produces achievement. Talent without effort remains potential; effort without talent can still produce great results.
A hierarchy of goals lets you be flexible about methods while being steadfast about direction. If one route closes, the gritty person finds another way to the same destination.
Deliberate practice, studied by Anders Ericsson, involves focused effort on specific weaknesses, with feedback and repetition. It is often uncomfortable, which is why few people sustain it.
Duckworth found that the grittiest people often move from interest to purpose: they see their work as contributing to others. Purpose sustains effort when interest alone would fade.
Her family rule balances commitment and choice: children choose their hard thing, but must finish what they start. It teaches perseverance without forcing a single path.

title: Think Again
author: Adam Grant · 2021
tag: The power of knowing what you don't know, and the courage to change your mind.
ideas: Preacher, prosecutor, politician

Grant observes that we often think like preachers, defending our beliefs; prosecutors, attacking others' beliefs; or politicians, seeking approval. All three keep us from learning. He urges a fourth mode: the scientist, who treats beliefs as hypotheses to test.
Confident humility

The ideal is not low confidence but confident humility: being sure of your ability to learn while being humble about what you currently know. It allows you to lead decisively while staying open to evidence.
Beware the overconfidence cycle

Grant describes the 'Mount Stupid' effect: beginners often feel most confident when they know least. Real expertise brings a clearer sense of what you do not know. Feeling certain is not the same as being right.
Build a challenge network
Most people gather a support network that encourages them. Grant recommends also building a challenge network: people you trust to point out your blind spots and question your thinking.
Change minds by asking, not telling
Drawing on motivational interviewing, Grant shows that people change their views more easily when they are asked open questions and helped to find their own reasons, rather than lectured or attacked.
Rethink your plans regularly
He recommends scheduling regular checkups on career and life plans. Plans made years ago reflect who you were then. Asking 'is this still right for me?' is not indecision; it is wisdom.
faith: Say: produce your proof, if you should be truthful. The Qur'an repeatedly asks for evidence and invites reflection rather than blind following. Imam al-Shafi'i is often reported to have said that his opinion is correct with the possibility of being wrong, and his opponent's is wrong with the possibility of being right. That is confident humility, expressed by a master jurist.
practices: Name one belief you hold strongly and ask: what evidence would change my mind?
Identify two people for your challenge network, and ask them for honest pushback.
In your next disagreement, ask three open questions before stating your view.
reflect: When did I last change my mind on something important?
Am I acting like a preacher, prosecutor, politician or scientist?
closing: Bring your proof, stay humble about what you know, and keep thinking again.

verses.ar: وَقَالُوا۟ لَن يَدْخُلَ ٱلْجَنَّةَ إِلَّا مَن كَانَ هُودًا أَوْ نَصَٰرَىٰ تِلْكَ أَمَانِيُّهُمْ قُلْ هَاتُوا۟ بُرْهَٰنَكُمْ إِن كُنتُمْ صَٰدِقِينَ
verses.en: And they say, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." That is [merely] their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof, if you should be truthful."

deep: Grant argues that most of us spend too much time in preacher, prosecutor or politician mode, protecting our views or seeking approval. Scientist mode treats beliefs as hypotheses, open to evidence, which makes learning possible.
Confident humility allows a leader to act decisively while remaining open to correction. It is the opposite of both arrogance and insecurity.

Grant draws on research showing that beginners often overestimate their knowledge. As expertise grows, confidence becomes more calibrated. The danger zone is early in learning, when confidence is high and knowledge is thin.

A challenge network includes people who disagree with you thoughtfully and are willing to point out flaws. It protects against blind spots, especially for leaders surrounded by people reluctant to contradict them.

Motivational interviewing is a method developed in counselling, where the helper asks open questions, listens and reflects, helping people find their own motivation to change. It often works better than argument.
Grant suggests regular checkups on life and career plans, as one would on health. Changing direction based on new information is not inconsistency but wisdom.

title: Range
author: David Epstein · 2019
tag: Why generalists often triumph in a specialised world.
ideas: Tiger versus Roger

Tiger Woods specialised in golf from early childhood. Roger Federer played many sports before focusing on tennis. Epstein argues that Federer's path, a period of sampling before specialising, is more common among top performers than the Tiger story suggests.
Kind and wicked learning environments

In 'kind' environments like chess or golf, rules are clear and feedback is fast, so early specialisation works. In 'wicked' environments, like business, policy and medicine, rules change and feedback is delayed. There, breadth and adaptability matter more.
Learning that sticks is slow
Research on 'desirable difficulties' shows that mixing different kinds of problems and struggling before getting the answer makes learning slower at first but much more durable and flexible.
Match quality
People who try different paths before committing tend to find work that fits them better, which Epstein calls match quality. Switching is often not failure but a search for fit.
Outsiders solve problems insiders cannot
Epstein shows examples of complex problems solved by people from outside the field, who brought analogies from elsewhere. Breadth gives you more tools and more ways of seeing.
Think in analogies
Generalists are good at drawing analogies between distant domains, which helps in solving novel problems. Reading widely and working across different roles builds this capacity.
faith: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of night and day are signs for those of understanding, who remember Allah standing, sitting and lying on their sides, and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth. The Qur'an invites reflection across the whole of creation. Islamic civilisation's great scholars, such as Ibn Sina, al-Biruni and Ibn Khaldun, were famous for their range across medicine, astronomy, history and theology.
practices: Read one article or book from a field far from your own this week.
Look for an analogy from another field for a problem you are stuck on.
Mix your learning: practise different types of problems in one session.
reflect: Is my work a kind or a wicked environment?
Where could my experience in one role help me in another?
closing: Sample widely, think in analogies, and reflect on the whole of creation. Range is a gift in a complex world.

verses.ar: إِنَّ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱخْتِلَٰفِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ لَـَٔايَٰتٍ لِّأُو۟لِى ٱلْأَلْبَٰبِ
verses.en: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day are signs for those of understanding -

verses.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يَذْكُرُونَ ٱللَّهَ قِيَٰمًا وَقُعُودًا وَعَلَىٰ جُنُوبِهِمْ وَيَتَفَكَّرُونَ فِى خَلْقِ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ رَبَّنَا مَا خَلَقْتَ هَٰذَا بَٰطِلًا سُبْحَٰنَكَ فَقِنَا عَذَابَ ٱلنَّارِ
verses.en: Who remember Allāh while standing or sitting or [lying] on their sides and give thought to the creation of the heavens and the earth, [saying], "Our Lord, You did not create this aimlessly; exalted are You [above such a thing]; then protect us from the punishment of the Fire.

deep: Epstein argues that the 'Tiger' story of early specialisation is less typical than we think. Many top performers, including Federer, sampled widely before settling on their field, developing broader skills that later helped them excel.

In kind environments, practice quickly builds intuition because feedback is clear and consistent. In wicked environments, like leadership or finance, the patterns are less stable, and broad knowledge helps people adapt to new situations.
Research cited by Epstein shows that interleaving, mixing different problem types, makes learning harder in the short term but more durable and transferable.
Epstein argues that switching paths is often a sign of learning what fits, not failure. Match quality, the fit between a person and their work, leads to greater commitment and success.

Outsiders can solve problems that insiders cannot, because they bring different analogies and fresh perspectives. Epstein gives examples of challenges posted online that were solved by people from unrelated fields.

Generalists build a store of analogies from different domains, which helps them see solutions others miss. Islamic scholars like Ibn Khaldun, combining history, law and economics, show the power of this breadth.

title: The Psychology of Money
author: Morgan Housel · 2020
tag: Doing well with money has less to do with intelligence and more to do with behaviour.
ideas: Behaviour beats intelligence

Housel tells of a janitor who quietly built a fortune of millions by saving and investing patiently for decades, and of a highly educated finance executive who went bankrupt through overspending and leverage. Money success is a soft skill: how you behave matters more than what you know.
Enough

The hardest financial skill, Housel argues, is getting the goalpost to stop moving. People with plenty sometimes risk everything they have for more they do not need. Knowing what is 'enough' protects you from ruin.
Compounding needs time

Most of Warren Buffett's wealth was accumulated after his sixties, not because of a secret formula but because he started early and kept going for decades. The key to compounding is not extraordinary returns; it is staying in the game for a long time.
Wealth is what you don't see

A luxury car shows that someone spent money, not that they have money. Real wealth is the assets not spent: savings, investments, options. It is invisible by nature, which is why it is so easy to misjudge.
Leave room for error
Plans fail. Housel urges a margin of safety: savings and flexibility that let you survive bad luck. The goal is not to maximise returns but to avoid being forced out of the game.
Save without a reason

You do not need a specific goal to save. Savings buy independence: the freedom to take a better job, handle an emergency, or say no. Control over your time, Housel argues, is the highest dividend money pays.
faith: And those who, when they spend, do so neither extravagantly nor stingily, but are ever between that, justly moderate. The Qur'an describes the servants of the Most Merciful as balanced in spending. Housel's 'enough' is the Islamic virtue of qana'ah, contentment. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that true richness is not abundance of goods, but richness of the soul, in a hadith in both Sahihs.
practices: Write down a number that would be 'enough' for your family's needs and security.
Set up an automatic monthly saving, however small.
Build an emergency buffer equal to three months of expenses over the next year.
reflect: Is my goalpost still moving?
What would I do with more control over my time?
closing: Be balanced, know what is enough, and give patience time to work.

verses.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ إِذَآ أَنفَقُوا۟ لَمْ يُسْرِفُوا۟ وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا۟ وَكَانَ بَيْنَ ذَٰلِكَ قَوَامًا
verses.en: And [they are] those who, when they spend, do so not excessively or sparingly but are ever, between that, [justly] moderate

deep: Housel tells the story of Ronald Read, a janitor and petrol station attendant who left an estate of about eight million dollars, built through simple saving and patient investing. The contrast with well-paid professionals who go bankrupt shows that behaviour, not income alone, decides financial outcomes.

Housel warns that risking what you have and need to gain what you don't need is a poor trade. Many financial disasters happen to people who already had enough but wanted more. Contentment is a protection, not just a virtue.

Buffett began investing as a child and kept going for decades, so time multiplied his returns. For ordinary savers, starting early and staying consistent through ups and downs matters more than finding perfect investments.

Housel notes we judge others' wealth by what they spend, not what they save. This drives social pressure to display rather than build. Avoiding that trap requires deliberately valuing what is invisible: security, savings and freedom.

A margin of safety, such as savings, low debt and flexibility, allows you to survive bad luck and stay invested long enough for compounding to work. Housel argues that survival is the foundation of long-term success.

Savings without a specific goal give control over your time and options when life changes unexpectedly. Housel considers independence, the ability to do what you want when you want, the greatest dividend money can pay.

title: The Richest Man in Babylon
author: George S. Clason · 1926
tag: Timeless money rules told through parables of an ancient city.
ideas: A part of all you earn is yours to keep

The central lesson of Clason's parables: of everything you earn, keep at least a tenth for yourself before paying anyone else. Most people pay the trader, the landlord and the tailor, but never themselves. Paying yourself first is how wealth begins.
Control your expenses
Clason warns that what we call 'necessary expenses' always grow to equal our income unless we deliberately resist. Budget so that you live on less than you earn, and separate true needs from desires.
Make your money work
Saved money should be put to work so that it grows. For a Muslim, this means halal investment, trade, partnership and productive assets, not interest-bearing lending, which the Qur'an prohibits.
Guard your treasure from loss

Clason advises investing only where the principal is safe, and seeking advice from those experienced in handling money. Many people lose savings by trusting enthusiasm over expertise. Protecting capital comes before chasing returns.
Own your dwelling and secure the future
He recommends making your home a productive investment rather than a lifelong rent, and providing for old age and for your family in case you are gone.
Increase your ability to earn
The last of his 'cures for a lean purse' is to grow your skills. The more valuable you become through learning and good work, the more you can earn and the more you can give.
faith: And do not make your hand as chained to your neck, nor extend it completely, lest you sit blamed and impoverished. The Qur'an asks for balance between hoarding and wasting. Clason's lessons on saving and wise investment are useful, but the Islamic version adds two essentials: wealth must be grown in halal ways, since Allah has permitted trade and forbidden riba, and it must be purified through zakah and charity.
practices: Set aside at least ten percent of your next income before any spending.
Review your 'necessary' expenses and cut one that is really a desire.
Seek advice from someone experienced before your next investment.
reflect: Am I paying everyone except my own future?
Is every part of my wealth grown in a halal way?
closing: Keep a part of what you earn, guard it, grow it in halal ways, and purify it with giving.

verses.ar: وَلَا تَجْعَلْ يَدَكَ مَغْلُولَةً إِلَىٰ عُنُقِكَ وَلَا تَبْسُطْهَا كُلَّ ٱلْبَسْطِ فَتَقْعُدَ مَلُومًا مَّحْسُورًا
verses.en: And do not make your hand [as] chained to your neck or extend it completely and [thereby] become blamed and insolvent.

deep: Clason's character Arkad teaches that saving even a tenth of income consistently builds wealth over time. The principle of paying yourself first means treating savings as a fixed obligation, not what is left after spending.
The parable warns that expenses tend to rise with income unless controlled. A budget that separates needs from desires prevents lifestyle inflation from consuming every increase.

In Islamic finance, money is made to work through trade, partnerships such as mudarabah and musharakah, and ownership of productive assets, sharing both profit and risk. This keeps the principle of growth while avoiding riba.
Clason's characters lose money by trusting inexperienced advisers. The lesson is to seek knowledgeable, honest counsel and to protect capital before seeking high returns.
Owning a home and providing for old age reduce long-term vulnerability. In Nigeria, where formal pensions may be limited, planning for future income is especially important.
Clason saw self-improvement as the final cure for poverty. Learning new skills and improving your work increases earning power and the capacity to give.

title: The Millionaire Next Door
author: Thomas J. Stanley & William D. Danko · 1996
tag: Most real millionaires don't look rich. They live below their means.
ideas: The rich often don't look rich

Stanley and Danko surveyed wealthy Americans and found that most did not drive luxury cars or live in mansions. Many were business owners who lived modestly in ordinary neighbourhoods. Visible consumption is a poor sign of actual wealth.
Big hat, no cattle
They borrowed a Texan expression for people who look wealthy but own little: big hat, no cattle. High income spent on status leaves little behind. Many high earners are financially fragile.
Accumulators and spenders

The authors divided people into prodigious accumulators of wealth, who have far more than expected for their income and age, and under accumulators, who have less. The difference was mainly in habits: budgeting, frugality and investing.
A simple measure

They offered a rough rule: your expected net worth is your age multiplied by your annual income, divided by ten. It is not exact, but it prompts an honest question: given what I earn, am I building wealth or just spending?
Don't fund adult children's lifestyles

They found that large ongoing gifts to adult children often reduced the children's own drive and wealth. Supporting education and independence, they suggested, helps more than subsidising consumption.
Time, energy and money go to what matters
Accumulators spend time planning finances and focus their energy on building assets, not on displaying them. Wealth is less about income than about allocation.
faith: Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion and adornment and boasting to one another and competition in increase of wealth and children. The verse names exactly what the study found: much spending is for adornment and boasting. A believer lives below his means not out of miserliness, but because his real wealth is what he sends ahead, and because display invites envy and arrogance.
practices: Calculate your net worth honestly, and compare it with the rough rule.
Postpone one status purchase for three months, and save the amount.
Plan support for your children that builds independence rather than dependence.
reflect: How much of my spending is for display?
Am I an accumulator or a spender?
closing: Real wealth is quiet. Live below your means, build what lasts, and send ahead what truly matters.

verses.ar: ٱعْلَمُوٓا۟ أَنَّمَا ٱلْحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنْيَا لَعِبٌ وَلَهْوٌ وَزِينَةٌ وَتَفَاخُرٌۢ بَيْنَكُمْ وَتَكَاثُرٌ فِى ٱلْأَمْوَٰلِ وَٱلْأَوْلَٰدِ كَمَثَلِ غَيْثٍ أَعْجَبَ ٱلْكُفَّارَ نَبَاتُهُۥ ثُمَّ يَهِيجُ فَتَرَىٰهُ مُصْفَرًّا ثُمَّ يَكُونُ حُطَٰمًا وَفِى ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةِ عَذَابٌ شَدِيدٌ وَمَغْفِرَةٌ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ وَرِضْوَٰنٌ وَمَا ٱلْحَيَوٰةُ ٱلدُّنْيَآ إِلَّا مَتَٰعُ ٱلْغُرُورِ
verses.en: Know that the life of this world is but amusement and diversion and adornment and boasting to one another and competition in increase of wealth and children - like the example of a rain whose [resulting] plant growth pleases the tillers; then it dries and you see it turned yellow; then it becomes [scattered] debris. And in the Hereafter is severe punishment and forgiveness from Allāh and approval. And what is the worldly life except the enjoyment of delusion.

deep: Stanley and Danko found that many millionaires owned modest homes and cars and worked in ordinary businesses. Their wealth came from consistent saving, careful spending and investment over decades.
High earners who spend heavily on status often have little net worth. The authors' phrase captures the gap between appearance and reality, a common pattern in societies that prize display.
Prodigious accumulators budget carefully, avoid unnecessary debt and invest regularly. Under accumulators often earn similar incomes but spend more, leaving little behind.

The rough formula is a prompt for reflection rather than a precise target. It encourages people to compare their savings with their earnings and age, and to ask whether their habits are building or eroding wealth.

The authors found that adult children receiving large ongoing financial gifts often became dependent. Helping children become self-sufficient, through education and modest support, tends to serve them better.
Wealth accumulators spend their time planning and investing rather than displaying. This aligns with the Islamic preference for moderation and with the warning against boasting in wealth.

title: Your Money or Your Life
author: Vicki Robin & Joe Dominguez · 1992
tag: Money is life energy. Spend it like it is.
ideas: Money is life energy

The authors define money as something we trade our life energy for: hours of our limited life. Every purchase can be measured in hours of life spent earning it. This reframing changes how we see small and large expenses.
Your real hourly wage

After subtracting the hidden costs of work, such as commuting, work clothes, stress-related spending and time spent recovering, many people earn far less per hour than they think. Knowing your real hourly wage makes spending decisions clearer.
Track every naira

The programme asks readers to track every unit of money coming in and going out for a month. Most people are surprised by where their money actually goes, and awareness alone begins to change behaviour.
The fulfilment curve

At first, spending increases fulfilment: survival, then comforts, then some luxuries. After a point, more spending brings less satisfaction and more clutter and worry. The peak of the curve is 'enough'.
Align spending with values
For each category of spending, ask: did I receive fulfilment in proportion to the life energy spent? Is this in line with my values? Small adjustments add up to a life that reflects what you believe.
Financial independence
As savings and investments grow, the income they produce can eventually cover expenses. The authors call this the crossover point, when work becomes a choice rather than a necessity.
faith: And spend from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says: my Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be among the righteous. Money is life energy, and life is limited. The Qur'an warns against hoarding until it is too late to give. The question 'is this worth the hours of my life?' becomes, for a believer, 'is this worth what I will answer for?'
practices: Track every expense for 30 days.
Calculate your real hourly wage after work-related costs.
For each spending category, ask if it matched its value in life energy.
reflect: Where is my spending out of line with my values?
What would I give if I knew my time was short?
closing: Every naira is an hour of your life. Spend it on what matters, and give before the chance passes.

verses.ar: وَأَنفِقُوا۟ مِن مَّا رَزَقْنَٰكُم مِّن قَبْلِ أَن يَأْتِىَ أَحَدَكُمُ ٱلْمَوْتُ فَيَقُولَ رَبِّ لَوْلَآ أَخَّرْتَنِىٓ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍ قَرِيبٍ فَأَصَّدَّقَ وَأَكُن مِّنَ ٱلصَّٰلِحِينَ
verses.en: And spend [in the way of Allāh] from what We have provided you before death approaches one of you and he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me for a brief term so I would give charity and be of the righteous."

deep: The authors encourage readers to calculate how many hours of life each purchase costs. A new phone might cost weeks of work. Seen this way, many purchases lose their appeal.
Hidden costs of work include commuting, special clothing, meals out and stress spending. Subtracting these from income gives a truer picture of how much each hour of work really earns.
Tracking every expense for a month, in naira or any currency, reveals spending patterns we might not notice. Awareness itself often reduces wasteful spending.
The fulfilment curve shows that beyond a certain point, extra spending does not increase happiness. Recognising 'enough' helps avoid the trap of endless consumption.
Aligning spending with values means asking whether each expense reflects what you care about: family, faith, health, learning. Small adjustments can bring spending and values into harmony.
The crossover point is when investment income covers living expenses. For Muslims, building towards it through halal investments offers freedom to devote more time to worship, family and service.

title: Al-Ghazali on the Purpose of Money
author: Imam al-Ghazali · Ihya 'Ulum al-Din
tag: Nine centuries ago, a theologian explained what money is for, and why hoarding and usury betray it.
ideas: Money is a judge between goods

In the Book of Gratitude in the Ihya, al-Ghazali explains that Allah created gold and silver coins, dinars and dirhams, so that very different goods, a camel and saffron, could be valued against each other. Money is a measure and a mediator, valued not for itself but for what it allows.
Like a mirror without colour

He compares money to a mirror, which has no colour of its own and therefore reflects all colours. Because money has no use in itself, it can represent the value of everything. That is its wisdom and purpose.
Hoarding imprisons the judge

Whoever hoards money, al-Ghazali wrote, is like someone who imprisons a ruler, preventing him from doing his work of judging between people. Money withdrawn from circulation fails its purpose, which is why the Qur'an condemns hoarding.
Usury misuses money

He argued that dealing in money for money, as in usury, treats the measure as if it were the goal. Money is created to be a means for trade and real exchange, not a commodity to be multiplied by itself.
Earning is worship when done rightly

Elsewhere in the Ihya, al-Ghazali praises honest trade, fair weights and kindness in dealings, and warns against cheating, hoarding food and exploiting need. The market, done rightly, is a place of worship.
Wealth is a test of gratitude

For al-Ghazali, gratitude for wealth means using it for its purpose: meeting needs, supporting family, giving charity and serving the community. Wealth used otherwise is ingratitude, however much one says alhamdulillah.
faith: And those who hoard gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allah: give them tidings of a painful punishment. Al-Ghazali's economic theory is a deep reading of this verse. Money is a trust with a purpose; circulation, fair trade and giving fulfil it, while hoarding and usury betray it. Islamic finance today, at its best, is an attempt to restore that original purpose.
practices: Review one asset you hold idle, and consider how it could circulate productively and lawfully.
Calculate your zakah carefully this year, with advice if needed.
Make one purchase this month that supports an honest local trader.
reflect: Is my money serving its purpose, or am I serving it?
How does my work in finance reflect al-Ghazali's view of money?
closing: Money is a mirror and a judge, not a master. Let it circulate, trade honestly, and spend it in the way of Allah.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِنَّ كَثِيرًا مِّنَ ٱلْأَحْبَارِ وَٱلرُّهْبَانِ لَيَأْكُلُونَ أَمْوَٰلَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلْبَٰطِلِ وَيَصُدُّونَ عَن سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ وَٱلَّذِينَ يَكْنِزُونَ ٱلذَّهَبَ وَٱلْفِضَّةَ وَلَا يُنفِقُونَهَا فِى سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِ فَبَشِّرْهُم بِعَذَابٍ أَلِيمٍ
verses.en: O you who have believed, indeed many of the scholars and the monks devour the wealth of people unjustly and avert [them] from the way of Allāh. And those who hoard gold and silver and spend it not in the way of Allāh - give them tidings of a painful punishment.

deep: Al-Ghazali's discussion comes in the Book of Gratitude in the Ihya. He explains that people need to exchange goods of different kinds, and money provides a common measure so that unequal things can be valued fairly.
The mirror image shows that money's value lies in what it represents, not in itself. Because it has no use of its own, it can stand in for the value of everything else.
Hoarding money, al-Ghazali argued, prevents it from fulfilling its role as a medium of exchange. This is why the Qur'an condemns those who hoard gold and silver without spending in the way of Allah.

For al-Ghazali, usury turns money from a means into a goal, generating wealth from money itself rather than from productive trade. This insight underpins the Islamic prohibition of riba and the emphasis on real economic activity.
Al-Ghazali praised honest merchants and warned against cheating, hoarding staple foods and exploiting people's need. Trade done with fairness and kindness becomes worship.

Gratitude for wealth means using it according to its purpose: meeting needs, supporting family, giving charity and serving the community. Misusing wealth, even while praising Allah, is a form of ingratitude.

title: How to Win Friends and Influence People
author: Dale Carnegie · 1936
tag: The classic guide to handling people with warmth, respect and sincerity.
ideas: Don't criticise, condemn or complain

Carnegie's first principle is that criticism makes people defensive and rarely changes them. Even people who have done wrong usually justify themselves. Understanding why people act as they do achieves far more than condemning them.
Give honest, sincere appreciation
People deeply want to feel important and valued. Carnegie distinguished sincere appreciation from flattery: one comes from the heart and is specific; the other is cheap and transparent.
A person's name is the sweetest sound
Remembering and using someone's name shows respect. Carnegie noted that people feel noticed when you take the trouble to learn and remember their names.
Be a good listener

You make more friends in two months by being interested in others than in two years by trying to get them interested in you. Ask questions, listen closely, and let people talk about what matters to them.
Avoid arguments and let others save face

Carnegie observed that the only way to win an argument is to avoid it, because even when you win, the other person resents losing. When correcting someone, help them save face, and admit your own mistakes quickly.
Talk in terms of the other person's interests
To persuade, start from what the other person wants. Show how your request helps them reach their goals. People are moved by their own needs, not by yours.
faith: And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan induces dissension among them. The Qur'an commands the best speech precisely because harsh words open the door to division. The Prophet, peace be upon him, remembered people's names, smiled, listened fully, and corrected gently, often without naming the person. Carnegie's principles are, in many ways, prophetic manners rediscovered.
practices: Go one full day without criticising anyone, at work or at home.
Give three specific, sincere appreciations this week.
In your next conversation, ask three questions before sharing your view.
reflect: Do people feel more important after talking with me?
Which argument should I have avoided?
closing: Say what is best. Appreciate sincerely, listen deeply, and let people keep their dignity.

verses.ar: وَقُل لِّعِبَادِى يَقُولُوا۟ ٱلَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَنُ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنَ يَنزَغُ بَيْنَهُمْ إِنَّ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنَ كَانَ لِلْإِنسَٰنِ عَدُوًّا مُّبِينًا
verses.en: And tell My servants to say that which is best. Indeed, Satan induces [dissension] among them. Indeed Satan is ever, to mankind, a clear enemy.

deep: Carnegie observed that even notorious criminals justified their actions. Criticism rarely changes people; it makes them defensive. Understanding motives and offering encouragement are more effective ways to guide behaviour.
Sincere appreciation must be honest and specific. Flattery is quickly detected and damages trust, while genuine praise for real effort or achievement motivates people.
Remembering names shows people they matter. In Nigerian culture, where respectful greeting is valued, using names and proper titles carefully builds goodwill.
Carnegie's principle of being interested rather than interesting is simple but powerful. People feel valued when we listen to them, and that respect opens relationships.
Carnegie recommended avoiding arguments, admitting mistakes quickly and letting others save face. These habits reduce conflict and build lasting cooperation.
Persuasion starts with understanding the other person's needs. Showing how your proposal helps them achieve their goals makes cooperation more likely.

title: Never Split the Difference
author: Chris Voss · 2016
tag: Negotiation lessons from a former FBI hostage negotiator.
ideas: Negotiation is emotional, not just logical
Chris Voss spent years as the FBI's lead international kidnapping negotiator. He argues that people are not purely rational; emotions drive decisions. Effective negotiators deal with feelings first.
Tactical empathy

Tactical empathy means understanding the other side's feelings and perspective, and showing that you understand, without necessarily agreeing. People who feel understood become less defensive and more willing to cooperate.
Mirroring and labelling

Mirroring is repeating the last few words someone said, which encourages them to keep talking. Labelling names their emotion: 'it seems like you're frustrated by the delays.' Both calm tension and reveal information.
Aim for 'that's right'

Voss says the breakthrough moment is when the other side says 'that's right', meaning they feel truly understood. 'You're right' is often just a way to end the conversation. Summarise their position until you hear 'that's right'.
Calibrated questions

Instead of saying no or making demands, ask open 'how' and 'what' questions: 'How am I supposed to do that?' or 'What's the biggest challenge you face?' These make the other side think about your constraints and solve the problem with you.
An accusation audit

Before a difficult conversation, list every negative thing the other person might think about you, and say them first: 'You probably think we're being unreasonable.' Naming fears early takes away their power.
faith: And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear. Allah sent Musa and Harun to Pharaoh, the most arrogant tyrant, with an instruction to speak gently. Tactical empathy is not weakness; it is the method Allah prescribed for the hardest negotiation in history. The Prophet's patience at Hudaybiyyah shows the same calm strength.
practices: In your next tense conversation, label one emotion you notice.
Use one calibrated 'how' question instead of saying no.
Before a hard meeting, write and open with a short accusation audit.
reflect: Do I deal with feelings first, or rush to facts?
When did someone last say 'that's right' to me?
