closing: Speak gently, understand deeply, and ask the questions that invite people to solve the problem with you.

verses.ar: فَقُولَا لَهُۥ قَوْلًا لَّيِّنًا لَّعَلَّهُۥ يَتَذَكَّرُ أَوْ يَخْشَىٰ
verses.en: And speak to him with gentle speech that perhaps he may be reminded or fear [Allāh]."

deep: Voss learned in hostage negotiations that people under stress respond to emotions before logic. Effective negotiators acknowledge feelings, which calms the situation and opens room for problem-solving.
Tactical empathy is understanding and naming the other side's perspective without necessarily agreeing. It builds trust and helps uncover the real issues behind a position.
Mirroring encourages people to say more, revealing information. Labelling emotions shows understanding and can defuse tension, making the other side more open.
Hearing 'that's right' indicates the other person feels understood. 'You're right' may simply be a way to end the conversation. Voss aims for genuine understanding as the basis for agreement.
Calibrated questions invite the other side to consider your constraints and help solve the problem. They give the other person a sense of control while guiding the conversation.
An accusation audit anticipates negative perceptions and addresses them openly. This reduces their power and builds credibility, making the other side more receptive.

title: Start with Why
author: Simon Sinek · 2009
tag: Great leaders inspire action by starting with purpose.
ideas: The golden circle

Sinek draws three circles: what you do, how you do it, and why you do it. Most organisations communicate from the outside in, starting with what. Inspiring leaders communicate from the inside out, starting with why.
People don't buy what you do
Sinek argues that people buy why you do it. Customers, staff and partners are drawn to organisations whose purpose they share. A clear why builds loyalty that price and features cannot.
Why speaks to the deeper brain

He links the golden circle to how the brain works: our capacity for feeling, trust and decision-making responds to purpose, while facts and figures appeal to analysis. That is why a decision can feel right before we can explain it.
Clarity, discipline and consistency
A why must be clear, the how must be disciplined, and the what must be consistent with both. When actions contradict the stated purpose, trust collapses.
Leaders are followed for what they believe

Sinek points to Martin Luther King Jr., who drew a quarter of a million people to Washington not with a plan but with a belief. People followed not for him, but for themselves, because they shared the belief.
When why goes fuzzy

As organisations grow, founders' purpose often fades, and the focus shifts to what and how: growth, metrics and competition. Sinek warns that this is when organisations lose their inspiration and start to struggle.
faith: Say: indeed, my prayer, my rites of sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, Lord of the worlds. This is the ultimate 'why'. Every 'what' of a believer's life, work, family, worship, can be anchored in it. The hadith of intention, that actions are judged by their intentions, is the golden circle in a single line.
practices: Write your personal 'why' in one sentence.
Write your team's or company's 'why', and check whether staff can say it.
Begin your next presentation with why, before what and how.
reflect: Do the people I lead know why we do what we do?
Is my daily 'what' consistent with my 'why'?
closing: Start with why, and let your why be for Allah, Lord of the worlds.

verses.ar: قُلْ إِنَّ صَلَاتِى وَنُسُكِى وَمَحْيَاىَ وَمَمَاتِى لِلَّهِ رَبِّ ٱلْعَٰلَمِينَ
verses.en: Say, "Indeed, my prayer, my rites of sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allāh, Lord of the worlds.

deep: The golden circle encourages leaders to communicate purpose first. People are inspired by the reasons behind actions, which gives meaning to the what and how.
Sinek argues that loyalty comes from shared beliefs. Organisations with a clear why attract customers and employees who identify with that purpose.
Sinek links the why to the parts of the brain responsible for feelings and decision-making. This explains why purpose-driven messages can motivate more than facts alone.
Clarity of why, discipline in how and consistency in what build trust. When actions contradict stated purpose, people lose faith in leadership.
Martin Luther King's 'I have a dream' speech inspired people with a vision of justice, not a policy plan. People followed because they shared the belief, not because of the details.
As organisations grow, they risk losing their founding purpose. Sinek encourages leaders to keep the why alive through stories, decisions and culture.

title: Crucial Conversations
author: Patterson, Grenny, McMillan & Switzler · 2002
tag: Tools for talking when the stakes are high, opinions vary and emotions run strong.
ideas: When conversations become crucial
A conversation becomes crucial when stakes are high, opinions differ and emotions are strong. These are the conversations we tend to handle worst, by avoiding them or by attacking.
The pool of shared meaning
Healthy dialogue fills a 'pool of shared meaning' with everyone's facts, opinions and feelings. The more that goes into the pool, the better the decision. Silence and aggression both drain it.
Start with heart

Before speaking, ask: what do I really want for myself, for the other person, and for the relationship? Under pressure, we drift into wanting to win or to punish. Returning to what we truly want keeps us on track.
Make it safe

People become defensive when they feel unsafe. Restore safety by establishing mutual purpose, showing you care about their goals, and mutual respect, showing you value them as a person. Apologise or clarify when you have been misunderstood.
Master your stories
Between seeing what happens and feeling something, we tell ourselves a story about it, often blaming others. Separate facts from your story, and consider other possible explanations.
Speak persuasively, not abrasively
The authors suggest a simple path: share your facts, tell your story, ask for others' views, talk tentatively, and encourage testing. Confident but open speech invites dialogue instead of defence.
faith: The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your brothers, and fear Allah that you may receive mercy. Reconciliation is a command, and it requires exactly these skills. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said, in a hadith recorded by Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, that reconciling between people is better than voluntary fasting, prayer and charity, because corrupted relations destroy religion.
practices: Before a crucial conversation, write what you really want for both of you and the relationship.
Separate one recent conflict into facts and the story you told yourself.
Open your next difficult discussion by stating mutual purpose.
reflect: Do I go silent or become aggressive under pressure?
Which relationship needs a crucial conversation now?
closing: Make it safe, start with heart, and make peace, for reconciliation is beloved to Allah.

verses.ar: إِنَّمَا ٱلْمُؤْمِنُونَ إِخْوَةٌ فَأَصْلِحُوا۟ بَيْنَ أَخَوَيْكُمْ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُرْحَمُونَ
verses.en: The believers are but brothers, so make settlement between your brothers. And fear Allāh that you may receive mercy.

deep: Crucial conversations involve high stakes, differing views and strong emotions. Recognising these moments helps people prepare and respond thoughtfully rather than reactively.
The pool of shared meaning grows as people share facts, feelings and opinions openly. A larger pool leads to better decisions and stronger commitment.
Starting with heart means focusing on what you really want for yourself, others and the relationship. This keeps conversations from becoming contests to win.
Making it safe involves showing mutual purpose and respect. When people feel safe, they share more openly, allowing problems to be solved together.
Separating facts from stories helps avoid unfair judgments. By questioning the stories we tell ourselves, we can respond more fairly to others.
The authors' STATE method encourages sharing facts first, explaining your conclusions, inviting others' views, speaking tentatively and being open to testing ideas.
